💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) introduced on Nov.
  • The Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction.
  • In GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) introduced on Nov. 19, prompting gamers everywhere to take the day off and indulge in a lawless land of hedonism and crime. Unsurprisingly, one of the first activities some people tried in the open world sandbox game was to fly a plane into a building. However, these antics haven't been producing the results many expected.

The Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction. Even so, there is particular sensitivity around the subject of crashing planes into buildings. The 9/11 attacks 25 years ago remain a pivotal moment in the U.S. consciousness, to such an extent that many people's minds immediately venture there when presented with a plane and a building.

In GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact. Previous Grand Theft Auto games also didn't allow planes to damage buildings. Nevertheless, some fans wondered if GTA 6 would skew this trend, particularly as it aims to feel realistic.

According to early gameplay clips, this doesn't seem to be the case. In a widely circulated clip by Twitch streamer Windpress, his character parachutes from a plane aimed at a building, only to watch the aircraft apparently pass harmlessly through it. Another popular GTA 6 gameplay video from @DiegoPalmaX highlighted a manned plane collide with a building but remain completely intact, slowly falling to the ground and even hitting another structure on the way down.

Such clips have drawn criticism from some Grand Theft Auto fans, who have commented on the lack of realism.

Sources indicate that "you can't commit 9/11 in gta 6…" wrote X user @eveisthebastard. "'realism' smh…".

"people will undoubtably say stuff like this doesnt really matter and i would usually agree but when literally all the hype for this game has been 'wow look at all the details there are ten trillion things being simulated' then yeah it really does matter," said @fbq_2.

Meanwhile, others have argued that it's reasonable for developer Rockstar Games to prevent players from recreating the 9/11 attacks.

"[The point of the game] is to commit crimes. Not be a terrorist," wrote @_MiisterJ. "Why would a game let you recreate 9/11?... Out of everything the game has to offer you draw the line at doing 9/11??".

Some have suggested that GTA 6's unusual interactions between planes and buildings may be the result of bugs. Launch day bugs are common in fresh video games, with developers often issuing patches to fix them later on. Considering the strange behaviour of GTA 6's planes, particularly when compared to GTA 5, the idea that these are errors seems like a reasonable theory.

Recent findings suggest that however, other social media customers have attributed the viral videos of pristine planes to a toggle in GTA 6's settings. Found under gameplay settings, GTA 6 includes a Reduced Vehicle Damage toggle which increases the amount of abuse your car or plane can take. Though it hasn't been confirmed that this setting was responsible for the nonsensical plane-building interactions seen in widely spread GTA 6 clips, activating it could theoretically help prevent vehicles from becoming deadly fireballs.

Recent findings suggest that further GTA 6 gameplay videos have supported suggestions that the viral clips are unusual by capturing more typically expected interactions between buildings and planes. A clip from Twitch streamer ohnePixel shows his small plane exploding after he flies it into a building, though like in GTA 5 the building itself remains undamaged. Another video shared on X by @muaxh03 shows a plane being destroyed after its left wing hits a building, killing the player character.

Sources indicate that in an interview with Love magazine, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson stated that GTA 6 attempts to balance realism with immersion, indicating that it may deviate where strict adherence to reality would make the game less fun. Whether this includes declining to realistically depict what happens when a jet flies into a highrise will likely become clearer as more people jump in to play. Recent findings suggest that nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.

Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the tech giant’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce. And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.”.

By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it:.

Sources indicate that “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”.

In a recent development, “Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.”.

Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again:.

Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together.

According to recent reports, “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.”.

Industry observers note that kress’ fresh catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?).

Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and stated “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment.

Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase, adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post.

And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot.

Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.

Paresh Dave contributed to this article.

#35921. Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form.
  • Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean.
  • It has been revealed that polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.

Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.

It has been revealed that polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.

Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how important the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.

Industry observers note that dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size.".

Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock.

Recent findings suggest that to explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.

Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.

It has been revealed that the results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.

The discovery indicates that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.

In a recent development, dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor.".

Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor.

Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.

In a recent development, for roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.

It has been revealed that however, the most important finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.

Industry observers note that genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.

This suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.

Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats.

The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.

Polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.

However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.

One example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.

Sources indicate that the problem is that these habitats cannot rapidly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, latest ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.

Prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.".

Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost.

It has been revealed that the discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.

An important question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?

According to recent reports, researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.

Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.

To investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is right now participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.

This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.

The findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.

  • Recent findings suggest that the opening film of this year’s IDFA documentary festival, “White Tiger Column” takes on a large, raw subject: the fostering of a resistance movement and mentality, from the ground up, in the wake of the 2021 coup that saw Myanmar’s latest, democratically elected government overthrown by the country’s army.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following vulnerable recruits through six weeks on a Myanmar People's Defense Force bootcamp, this year's IDFA opener is an accomplished debut for Canadian filmmakers Robert Mentov, Dwight Jantzi and Bryan Dickie.

A nasal R&B jam by Justin Bieber isn’t everyone’s idea of comfort listening, least of all played on a crackly phone speaker. But when the singer’s 2020 hit “Intentions” plays midway through “White Tiger Column,” briefly bonding two teen female soldiers in a moment of bubbly release and actual acting-their-age joy, it’s like a shot of oxygen to Robert Mentov, Dwight Jantzi and Bryan Dickie‘s subtly upsetting documentary. Later on, Taylor Swift’s “You Belong With Me” likewise sticks out like a sweet, sore thumb in the film’s otherwise severe milieu: a remote Burmese jungle camp where GenZ volunteer recruits in the Myanmar People’s Defense Force are put through their paces, in the hope of standing up to the country’s military junta. It’s an unduly weighty calling at such a tender age; youth must occasionally, giddily assert itself. Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Blitz to Begin With Robert Downey Jr., Guillermo del Toro and Steven Spielberg as Moderators Matt Damon Reveals Wife Suffered a Brain Aneurysm and Had Surgery the 'Week Before the Oscars' Where 'Oppenheimer' Won Best Picture.

Recent findings suggest that the opening film of this year’s IDFA documentary festival, “White Tiger Column” takes on a large, raw subject: the fostering of a resistance movement and mentality, from the ground up, in the wake of the 2021 coup that saw Myanmar’s latest, democratically elected government overthrown by the country’s army. But it does so with delicate humanity, its focus less on collective rhetoric and conflict than on the many individual fragilities and growing pains within an improvised, makeshift corps. Spanning six weeks of basic training, the film doesn’t limn a neat coming-of-age arc: Nobody enters the camp a boy and leaves a man, but this underdog army works with the inexperienced rebels they have.

Industry observers note that A directorial collaboration between Dickie — a Canadian photographer specializing in sites of sociopolitical upheaval — and compatriots Jantzi and Mentov, founders of the hitherto more fiction-oriented Nocte Films studio, “White Tiger Column” takes an approach between the journalistic and the more ambiently observational. There are no talking-head interviews or information beyond some scene-setting title cards, but a patient sense of human interest prevails, as the filmmakers embed themselves in the camp for a full course of training, observing its process without interference. The human subjects are not named, but personalities and personal crises emerge from a rigid, would-be military routine.

In some senses, “White Tiger Column” follows a structure familiar from many a basic-training drama, as unformed young people reckon with the newly introduced strictures and challenges of army life. But the stakes here are very different, not least because everyone present is there by dint of their own urgent belief — having fled to the jungle to escape the reach of the country’s actual military overlords. “To fight the government, we must become soldiers ourselves,” they are reminded by their commanders, who have little more authority or experience than the recruits they’re leading. And the goal here is not mere national service or self-improvement: “I don’t want to just train, I want to fight,” notes one newcomer, speaking for many of his peers who can’t wait to get their hands on a weapon.

According to recent reports, in other respects, however, they’re just kids, and their vulnerability and naïveté are all the more exposed by these extreme circumstances. “I miss my bed, my fridge, my TV, my mom and dad,” indicates one, sounding less like a soldier than a homesick child at a summer camp — which the boot camp quite frequently resembles, with its tranquil setting, team-building, fireside bonding and weekly calls home. Less so the lessons in homemade explosives and rite-of-passage tattooing: adult reminders of the grim responsibilities and dangers that await them after a too-brief education in the ways of war. Upon completing their training, an instructor tells them: “From now on, we are comrades, though you may call me teacher if you wish.” In the resistance, ultimately, everyone’s just figuring it out.

It has been revealed that it’s tough-minded but not without stray moments of tenderness and joy — particularly when focused on the friendship between two intrepid female recruits, a conspicuous minority in the collective — or of lush cinematic beauty, as Mentov, also the film’s accomplished DP, can hardly fail to capture the verdant, shadow-streaked riches of the environment around them. But the filmmakers aren’t inclined to romanticize matters, either in terms of character-based narratives or ideological emphasis: In this simultaneously stirring and frightening portrait, we know exactly what everyone’s fighting for, but as one near-child soldier admits, “we only have theories about what might happen.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this holiday season, major-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.

"We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these significant-ticket items we have seen in history," noted Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.

Weinswig remarked retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.

"It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig said. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year.".

The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.

According to recent reports, according to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.

In a recent development, industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.

At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.

Recent findings suggest that most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit newly introduced record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.

Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology tech giant OneRail, which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's.

"You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania said.

It has been revealed that retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?

It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives said.

According to recent reports, UPS CEO Carol Tomé remarked on the firm's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers.".

Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for significant-box stores and major retailers, mentioned retailers are cautious.

"When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers said.

Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Firm's annual forecast. Leathers said even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.

Industry observers note that "The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers said. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf.".

ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.

It's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding upcoming team members.

Industry observers note that "Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there's better unit economics out there," Catania remarked.

Industry experts said they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.

A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would "drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry.".

Amit Regev, CEO of drone tech giant Flytrex, said the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.

"The expectation now is becoming so much more instant," Regev said.

Retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe's in September said it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing. Amazon earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.

Flytrex presently delivers for Walmart and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John's.

"Customers are looking for that instant gratification," Regev stated. "So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that's a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before he was Dustin, Stranger Things‘ adorably dorky, cap-wearing kid whose knack for science would help defeat interdimensional villains Vecna and the Mind Flayer, Gaten Matarazzo was a real theater kid.

In a recent development, aged nine, his first-ever professional credit was in the Broadway production of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert, and his second sizeable stage spell came just two years later, when Matarazzo joined the U.S.’ 25th Anniversary Tour of Les Misérables as neglected street child Gavroche. He would reprise the role in 2014’s Tony-nominated revival in Upcoming York (when the Connecticut-born actor was still only 12 years old). Related Stories Movies "Wicker Nipples" and All: 'Wicker' Cinematographer Celebrates Steamy Film's Viral Success Movies Indigenous Queer Drama 'Princess' Is Dedicated to "Everyone Fighting for Their Freedom, Their Identity".

According to recent reports, matarazzo’s household-name status wouldn’t come via these live performances, but through Netflix’s most successful original series of all time. At 24, Matarazzo is both hyper-aware of this fact and refreshingly liberated by it: Dustin, Stranger Things and its franchise-spawning, billion-streams success have allowed this now-very-adult actor — and astonishingly brilliant singer — to return to the art form he grew up entrenched in.

In a recent development, “It’s really lovely to have [Stranger Things] in our back pockets as we go forward in whatever we choose to do,” indicates Matarazzo over Zoom about his co-stars Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, Caleb McLaughlin, Noah Schnapp and Sadie Sink. “I’ve gravitated towards theater for now, just because it’s a reminder of my childhood, and I love it very, very much.”.

It’s fitting then that Matarazzo’s West End debut — and first major role since the final outing of the Duffer brothers’ Netflix tentpole — is in a show so close to his heart. Director Luke Sheppard (Paddington: The Musical) has seemingly bottled the energy of a late 20th-century New York City and unleashed it on the Tom Stoppard Theatre stage through an invigorating young cast. Jonathan Larson’s musical chronicles a year in the life of a group of impoverished 20-something artists and activists in the East Village. Their creative dreams are kept alive through song and a sense of punk enthusiasm as drug addiction, poverty, gentrification, and the HIV/AIDS epidemic loom large. Larson’s creation itself comes with built-in tragedy — the prodigious composer, lyricist and playwright died at 35 on the morning of Rent‘s first preview performance.

Below, Matarazzo dives into his masterful portrayal of aspiring filmmaker and story narrator Mark Cohen in this epic Rent rebirth. He tells The Hollywood Reporter about championing the “essential” stories of those with HIV/AIDS in late ’80s New York, why he believes he’s come out of the Stranger Things bedlam in one piece and what to expect from Lin-Manuel Miranda’s hotly anticipated Octet movie with Rachel Zegler, Amanda Seyfried, Tramell Tillman, Jonathan Groff and Sheryl Lee Ralph: “The things I want to do are probably things that I read and say, ‘I’ve never read anything like this before,’ and that’s what Octet was.”.

How did this all come together? Did the production approach you for Mark?

Yeah, they did. Luke specifically, which is very nice. It was very unexpected. […] I remember I was in the shower, and I got a notification as I was stepping out, and I wasn’t even dressed by the time I was on the phone and saying, “Yes, yes, yes!” because all I saw [was] the subject title: “Mark West End” and I didn’t know what it meant. I saw Luke’s name and I didn’t really know what the implications were, how long it would be, if it was truly a West End run, or if it was just going to be a London concert. But I knew that an opportunity to jump into the show was one that you don’t pass up, especially when it’s a director like Luke. So it was just a no-brainer. After I had given an immediate yes to being a part of it, then [came] the implication of moving away from home for an extended period of time, which I’ve done before, but never for this long and never by myself. […] Thankfully, I was working on some other stuff in the city leading up to it, so I actually got to meet some of the creative team for Rent.

You have a long-running relationship with Broadway. What were your preconceptions about the West End? Did you always want to perform here at some point?

In a recent development, absolutely. London is the birthplace of what modern theater looks like, and if you want to have a real grasp of, I think, the epitome of theater culture — and if you have the opportunity to — you should see shows in London. It’s easier said than done. I was always here for press for Stranger Things, which was very nice, but that’s really the only time I was ever able to come here. And on press runs and junkets, you rarely have any time to really enjoy the city. I knew how intimidating a process it was going to look like. I know how seriously it’s taken. I know how seriously audiences take it in New York and in London, and there is a standard that is expected to be met, which is warranted, so there is a pressure that comes along with that, especially coming from overseas. […] There’s always going to be a curiosity about somebody who isn’t necessarily known for having a bulk of work in theater jumping into something as intense as this. I was scared that there were going to be more eye rolls than optimism, and I was met with nothing but love, which was really, really wonderful.

It has been revealed that the energy in the room was just lovely. There were no eye rolls — only enthusiasm.

According to recent reports, and what was your relationship like with this show? Do you remember seeing Rent for the first time?

In a recent development, I remember being introduced to the show at a time when seeing it in its best form was hard to do. Because I was too young to see it when it was running on Broadway, but by the time I was old enough, not enough time had passed for a major professional production to really hit Fresh York again. A lot of time, after shows close, they need time to breathe. They need some time to simmer with new audiences so you can find new opportunities. You can gauge culturally what is resonating about a piece. […] But something that’s so special about Rent is that it was the modern musical. It was one of the first defining young, pop-rock shows that rolled out a new wave of theater kids. Rent was essential in bringing in a new wave of people who were going to love this form of art. And I remember when I first started getting into it, the movie had already been made. The show was already very famous. It had already closed on Broadway, so really, my introduction was scouring the internet to try to find as much information about it and as much footage as I could. And thankfully, they had a really great proshot [a high quality-recording] of the closing company, and it was stunning. […] That’s what led me to really feel an intense, real desire to one day get to do it at some point.

I recall reading that you have an uncle who was a closeted gay man in New York in the ’80s and ’90s, when the HIV/AIDS crisis was rife. We’re past that stigma now, but this is a show that manages to really capture the sentiment around that awful time.

In a recent development, yeah. It’s essential that stories about it and stories about the people who endured it, people we lost, people we still have, [are told]. It’s essential that it’s a continuation because the people that suffered through it and endured through it and thrived through it are still very much here, very much contributing to every walk of life, especially art and the theater. And that’s why this show just continues to work — because people don’t forget. As far as a musical goes, 30 years is a long time. But as far as a pandemic goes, 30 years is not a long time. […] They don’t cover it in American public schools as much as they should. I think they should. There’s a different lens that you learn about when you’re growing up in a time when it is significantly more treatable than it was.

In a recent development, in places where modern medicine is accessible, an HIV diagnosis is always going to be scary, but there are so many options. There are so many ways to prevent. There are so many ways to protect. It’s incredible that we’ve gotten to this point, but to hear it from people who were genuinely just terrified at not knowing how one gets it, how one spreads it, and what the timeline looks like for the rest of their life… Because there are people who would receive a diagnosis, and of course they could live 30, 40 years and never even experience symptoms. And then there were people who were dead in six months, and there was really no way to tell. I remember hearing about that and having this pit of dread. And even at nine or 10 years old, learning about that, that’s always scary, no matter what. But then you look around at people you respect and admire, and love very, very much, who can tell you personal stories about their own, not just watching their loved ones go through it, but then personally experiencing that. That is something that, even at that age, I didn’t take for granted.

And what’s amazing about Rent is that it’s framed by such radical optimism and a real punk enthusiasm. And it still resonates with audiences, which I’m sure you see every night.

Sources indicate that right? It’s a show that’s so full of love and so full of optimism, and it doesn’t talk down. It’s so beautiful to watch because it was a crisis and is a crisis, so there is always going to be a very large, very sad group of people who insist on making shame the central point of the conversation around that crisis. For this show to release at a time when that was still very present, where mass media wouldn’t cover it. […] Hindsight’s 2020. We can look back now and say, “Insane that it ever happened.” […] But to have the characters suffering through it [and] be some of the most vibrant, loving, enthusiastic, incredible people you could ever… Everybody has their issues. But after you watch the show and see the family that they create, all you want to do is be a part of it.

Industry observers note that you’ve had a little space from Stranger Things and Dustin now. When you reflect on it all, what feelings come up for you?

I don’t feel very far removed from it in the slightest. I know it’s been some time. [… But] there’s always a latest wave of people being like, “Oh, there’s that gem of a show that people talked about.” So I’m seeing friends of mine and people around my age, or even a little younger, even older, start this new wave of experiencing it for the first time, and that’s an incredible reminder because that’s something I had forgotten that was so special — seeing people be consistently surprised by the show in those early years, and that was before a standard was set, before an expectation had been made after the second or third season, which there always is going to be when a show does well.

It’s great to hear you talk positively about it all. We’ve seen how difficult child fame can be. It sounds like you’ve come out relatively unscathed.

It has been revealed that thanks. Kids can’t do this personally, but it’s a matter of ensuring that you are surrounded by people who have your best interests at heart, which I do, and others don’t. And a lot of times, that’s luck of the draw, and I was very lucky. My parents always made sure that I was doing it for the right reasons. My parents would always not just tell me but show me that they were invested in that process for the right reasons. Because they knew I loved it. And we were lucky with the team on the show specifically. There was a lot of prioritization of our safety and security and our education, and ensuring that we were enjoying ourselves throughout that process. I can only speak for myself, but I would assume that I can speak for [others]. Collectively, we had a really great experience, and we loved the show, and it was the best learning experience in the world that one could ask for. It’s like the best film school you could ever ask for.

Absolutely — on a show that enormous.

To work on a production in a show as intense as that was, you got to see every single day how something that massive is made. You gain a literacy in film and TV that you wouldn’t really get to learn otherwise, and we didn’t even know we were learning it. We didn’t even know that it was cementing itself into the backs of our brains. So now that we enter our early 20s, when most people are starting their careers in this world and just getting a gauge, there’s a weird little kind of mentality. I’m like, “Ah, back in the day…”.

You’re already weary and weathered!

Sources indicate that (Laughs.) Right! Jaded and sad. No, it’s really lovely to have that in our back pockets as we go forward in whatever we choose to do. I’ve gravitated towards theater for now, just because it’s a reminder of my childhood, and I love it very, very much. But I very much expect to continue working in film in different capacities. I see all of my friends doing incredible work in such different, wonderful ways, and none of us would really be able to do that without the opportunities we were given from the show.

I read that some people have been coming to Rent in Stranger Things costume and you’ve had to set a boundary?

According to recent reports, oh, goodness gracious! That was more of a thing in passing that I think was blown out of proportion a little bit. It was said in a more sarcastic, joking manner. But I’m okay with the way the sentiment was perceived because what was highlighted at the end was the emphasis on 20 other people being up on the stage that I’m on. […] That was more something that had happened once or twice, maybe in some other shows that I had done, and it’s more of a funny aside rather than this glitch that keeps becoming apparent.

I understand. There’s an entire ensemble alongside you. So people have to be considerate of that if they’re showing up just for you.

The gang that they have assembled is essential to why the show works. I remove myself from that completely. The people that I watch every day do the show are absolutely astounding, and they bring new life [and] spontaneity. They take the history of what the show means and transform it into something really, really fresh and beautiful. [We] were always going to be on the backs of the original tech giant that did this show, but the minute we all entered that room, we understood that there was going to be a new dynamic. We would have to develop a history that we, as individuals, all had with each other, and it was so surprisingly easy because of how engaged and full of life and excitement this whole company is. That’s before even mentioning that I’ve never heard this show sound the way it sounds when I’m listening to that group singing.

How have you found a West End audience compared to a Broadway one?

It has been revealed that the thing that’s different about this is [that] Rent will always feel like a Broadway show. It feels like major, booming Broadway, and I think that transfers over here, and audiences come in with that energy. So it feels like a very New York audience when we’re doing the show. I was warned that you have to earn [a wild reaction] more here. But there’s this energy with this show being here and being created here. I think that almost feels like there’s this brewing excitement about it when we go in.

It has been revealed that it feels like one of the only times when it’s really cemented itself as a new type of show, a new type of Rent. I think we’re very early in the run, but succeeding pretty substantially here… This feels like one of the ones where it’s like, “Oh shit, they tried something, and that thing that they’re trying is working.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s clicking. It must be so satisfying to know that it’s landed. Because those first few weeks are nervy, right?

According to recent reports, in terms of what’s next… You have Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Octet coming up. Does Rent mark a latest chapter for you?

I think so. I don’t know. It would be a weird thing to label. I just want to take things in [my] stride and go with the flow of what presents itself over time. I don’t really want to force anything. I’m doing a lot of theater right now because those opportunities have presented themselves, and it [was] a no-brainer that I wanted to continue doing it. But it’s not like I’ll finish up this run and be like, “Now I’m doing movies, so don’t fucking ask me to do [anything else].” You know what I mean? Like, whatever comes up that I find to be an opportunity for growth and learning… I really only want to learn. I rarely want to do things I’ve done before, and that’s why I decided to do this because it’s a latest experience in a new city, and a workload that I hadn’t really tackled that intensely yet.

According to recent reports, I knew it was going to be a physical challenge, and that’s what I was going to learn from this process. But as far as film and TV goes, I heard this once, and I can’t attribute this thought to myself because Rob Pattinson noted it once in an interview. (Laughs.) He really considers whether he can read a script and say, “If I say no, I have to be okay with never doing the script again.” Because there’s a lot of things that come through. and it’s like, I’ve seen this before. It’s great. It’s good. I just saw this yesterday, or I’ve done this before, [or] that’ll probably be very good, and there’s going to be good people making it, but I don’t think I’ll learn much from that experience. The things I want to do are probably things that I read and say, “I’ve never read anything like this before,” and that’s what Octet was.

In a recent development, it was a blending of worlds that I love so much. It’s a beautiful score. Dave Malloy is an incredible writer. Lin’s an incredible director. The cast that was involved — working with each individual in that group has been a goal and dream of mine for a long time. So for them to all be in the room at the same time… And as far as a movie goes, I love this. I mean, it’s so weird, and I’m obsessed with it. I love weird shit. I like filming things that are weird, and I feel like permission is granted if you’re doing something that is very, very absurd, which, at times, this movie is. It grants you personal permission to be as absurd as you can, and that’s when I feel most comfortable jumping out of my comfort zone — when everybody else is also doing it.

Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth.
  • The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR).
  • Industry observers note that the stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer upcoming clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

Industry observers note that the stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

Until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses.

The newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

Sources indicate that despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.

Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

In a recent development, the latest discovery provides an important breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," stated lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.

McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away.

In a recent development, the radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

According to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.

The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface.".

A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.".

Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair.

ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.

The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," remarked Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

In a recent development, after the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.

The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.

The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

Sources indicate that both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

It has been revealed that dr. McSweeney said, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.".

The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion.".

Sources indicate that materials provided by International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable organization in the space of a month.

It has been revealed that since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the company's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.".

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

Sources indicate that the committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.

The manufacturer did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was confirmed hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that "Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great manufacturer," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea.".

Sources indicate that trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

In a recent development, huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.

Recent findings suggest that that tech giant, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

  • Sources indicate that "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines," ULA wrote in an patch today (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Launch Alliance (ULA) is getting a handle on why its Vulcan Centaur rocket failed over the weekend.

Industry observers note that that failure, which occurred during a launch from Florida's Space Coast on Sunday (Nov. 15), led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites. ULA soon traced the anomaly to Vulcan Centaur's first stage, and it has now pinpointed the problem area even further.

Sources indicate that "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines," ULA wrote in an patch today (Nov. 18).

This is good news for Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos' aerospace tech giant, which builds the BE-4. Two of these engines power Vulcan's first-stage booster, and they're also key to Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket: That heavy lifter features seven or nine BE-4s in its first stage, depending on the configuration. (New Glenn has its own issues at the moment; it exploded during a test on May 28, and Blue Origin is working to return the powerful rocket to flight.).

In a recent development, ULA had already said that Vulcan's six solid rocket boosters (SRBs) and its Centaur V upper stage — which employs a different engine, the RL-10 — seem to perform well on Sunday. Further analysis is firming up that conclusion, according to today's enhancement.

Vulcan has had concerns with its SRBs in the past. On the rocket's second and fourth flights — which rolled out in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds into flight. On both occasions, Vulcan overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payload to orbit.

In the wake of the February flight, ULA and Northrop Grumman, which builds the SRBs, tweaked the nozzle design — a fix that apparently worked, based on Sunday's nominal performance.

Sources indicate that sunday's launch was the fifth ever for the two-stage Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has now experienced issues on three of its five flights, though Sunday's was the only one that ended in failure.

Industry observers note that vulcan was out of action for about nine months after the February SRB matter. It's unclear how long its current grounding will last; that depends on what ULA's anomaly investigation, which the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing, ends up finding.

In a recent development, michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz.   • It has been revealed that speaking on a panel at the Doha Industry Days, the industry program of the Doha Film Festival, Hwang was asked what would be next in the world of “Squid Game.” “Unfortunately, it’s not mine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emmy-winning director Hwang Dong-hyuk remarked he believes he will "someday" return to the hit franchise while speaking about its massive success at the Doha Industry Days.

Hwang Dong-hyuk, the Emmy-winning creator and director of Netflix‘s global phenomenon “Squid Game,” remarked he intends to “someday” return to the story that launched him into international stardom. As it stands, “Squid Game” officially ended with Season 3 in 2025, with Hwang himself confirming the end of the series. Netflix has already launched a spin-off, “Squid Game: The Challenge,” with the rumor mill swirling around other possible expansions, including a U.S. remake. Related Stories From a Mockbuster Version of 'The Odyssey' to a 'Jiu-Jitsu Nun': How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming (and Even Lower Budgets) 'The Odyssey' Oscar Blitz to Begin With Robert Downey Jr., Guillermo del Toro and Steven Spielberg as Moderators.

It has been revealed that speaking on a panel at the Doha Industry Days, the industry program of the Doha Film Festival, Hwang was asked what would be next in the world of “Squid Game.” “Unfortunately, it’s not mine. I don’t own ‘Squid Game.’ Netflix owns the IP, so it’s not my decision how to expand,” he noted.

It has been revealed that “As far as I’m concerned, someday I’ll get back to ‘Squid Game,'” he added. “When I have a great idea, I’ll make another one.”.

Recent findings suggest that for now, Hwang is focused on his next feature film, “K.O. Club.” The project will reunite the director with “Squid Game” star Lee Byung-hun, joined in the cast by fellow franchise alum Park Hae-soo, Oh Jung-se (“It’s Okay to Not Be Okay”), Cho Yeo-jeong (“Parasite”) and Kim So-jin (“The Man Standing Next”). Firstman Studio, the production firm Hwang runs with producer Kim Ji-yeon, who also goes by Jenny Kim, confirmed the casting, with filming targeted for the first half of 2027.

It has been revealed that “K.O. Club” is a dystopian sci-fi set around 20 years in the future, where the rich can buy youth. In that scenario, an increasingly desolate and disgruntled young generation starts the titular “Killing Old Men Club” to organize assassinations of the wealthy and powerful over 80. “I believe the world is getting worse and worse,” Hwang stated of the inspiration behind the project.

“People live longer because of technology and science, so they are not dying,” he added. “Maybe they’ll [get to] live to 150 years old. The rich never go away. They grab the power and money in their hands, which means the younger generation has nothing to do; they have no power, no money, no jobs.”.

Hwang said the effect on young people is already visible, pointing to “all those riots in Paris and everywhere.”.

Hwang and Kim spoke at length about the surreal experience of seeing their series blow up into one of Netflix’s most-watched reveals ever, a global sensation that defined culture in the pandemic years. “After the major reaction from the global audience and the success that followed, as a producer, I faced a new challenge and environment,” said Kim. “Most of the people, all the people except for the main character, died during the game [in the first season], so the biggest challenge was to develop the new story with new people.”.

Industry observers note that “There was pressure from Netflix,” Kim or Hwang said of Season 2, which arrived three years after Season 1. “We needed to deliver it fast, and the global audience was waiting for the next season. We were always getting questions: ‘Where is Season 2? Season 3?’ It was a nightmare.”.

Sources indicate that the team kept the production process the same across seasons, Kim said, largely to meet the expectations of “Squid Game” fans all over the world. “What was it that fans liked about ‘Squid Game’? We tried to maintain that.”.

In a recent development, hwang mentioned he never tries to “make something that people like.” “I always try to make what I like to make while at the same time hoping and praying people like what I like to make. If I lose that mindset, I’ll go crazy.”.

In a recent development, “When I first wrote the script, the beginning point of my creative process was when I was poor,” he recalled. “I didn’t have much money and imagined: What if it was me? Would I enter this kind of competition and try to win the prize? I was so broke in 2009. I was so broke. I only had like $5 in my account.”.

In a recent development, hwang recalled reading Japanese comics and manga about survival games where the tasks were “mentally, intellectually, and physically difficult.” “A guy like me could not survive [it]. I started thinking like that. What if there was something where a normal guy like me could not only compete but become a winner? That’s how I developed the idea of ‘Squid Game.'”.

Because Season 1 was so well received by a global audience, Hwang said, he had the self-belief that Seasons 2 and 3 would also be loved. “I tried to brainwash myself throughout the creative process.”.

“I felt more free to do things my own way,” he added. “I believe that the success of the first series, whatever the previous success was, was leverage, an asset, to be able to take bigger risks. When you have massive success, everybody believes you. No matter what you say, they say I love it. That’s when you take a big risk in your life. That’s the only chance.”.

As for what’s next for Firstman Studio, Kim said the company’s credibility went up after “Squid Game,” but that it remains a very small company. “We’re not making a lot of projects. The reason we want to do this is that, as an independent producer, rather than focusing on profitability, we want to focus on taking the right creative risks to create what we believe in.”.

#35910. MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1705 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • Researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • Industry observers note that the findings raise notable questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But latest research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

Industry observers note that the findings raise notable questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

It has been revealed that "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

In a recent development, the study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

Deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

In a recent development, in 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an notable role in carrying away waste products.

Recent findings suggest that that earlier discovery led to a new question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

Sources indicate that previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially vital.

It has been revealed that to investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Recent findings suggest that each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

In a recent development, the researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings demonstrated that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

The researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

It has been revealed that when a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

It has been revealed that to measure this response, the researchers demonstrated volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

In a recent development, in many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Recent findings suggest that participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

According to recent reports, once again, the older group showed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

It has been revealed that using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes claims. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have vital implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

Recent findings suggest that none of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants showed signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

The relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

In a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

Sources indicate that while older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

Recent findings suggest that "It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis notes. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

Novo notes Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial
