💡 Key Takeaways
  • Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.
  • In a recent development, wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo.
  • Recent findings suggest that when evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

In a recent development, wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

Recent findings suggest that when evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

It has been revealed that "This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

In a recent development, in Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

Recent findings suggest that but more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina stated.

Novo noted Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.

"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

#35907. Anthony Boyle on Becoming Sam Bankman-Fried for ‘The Altruists’ and Finding the Grey in History’s Villains: ‘I’ve Played More Real People Than Not’

Anthony Boyle on Becoming Sam Bankman-Fried for ‘The Altruists’ and Finding the Grey in History’s Villains: ‘I’ve Played More Real People Than Not’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A little over 10 years ago, Anthony Boyle was about to celebrate his first major screen role.
  • Industry observers note that in Nick Hamm’s road trip drama about Northern Ireland’s peace process, Boyle — who grew up in a predominantly Catholic neighbourhood in West Belfast — was playing a young Ian Paisley, the fire-and-brimstone Protestant minister once described as a “foghorn on legs” (by Ozzy Osbourne, no less).
  • “And they cut me from it!” he states with a laugh, speaking from an upmarket gym in central London with a street entrance so discreet it’s impossible to find without assistance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A little over 10 years ago, Anthony Boyle was about to celebrate his first major screen role. It wasn’t a huge part, but “The Journey” was a sizeable career leg-up for the Northern Irish actor, then barely out of drama school and with a resume largely led by a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it appearance on “Game of Thrones.” It was also a subject extremely close to home.

Industry observers note that in Nick Hamm’s road trip drama about Northern Ireland’s peace process, Boyle — who grew up in a predominantly Catholic neighbourhood in West Belfast — was playing a young Ian Paisley, the fire-and-brimstone Protestant minister once described as a “foghorn on legs” (by Ozzy Osbourne, no less). With the film premiering in Venice, it was the perfect introduction. Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 Upcoming Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs Tarantino Fired Mélanie Laurent From 'Inglourious Basterds' After 'Terrible' Table Read and Axed Isabelle Huppert for Not Showing Up: 'I Don't Owe You Jack S---'.

“And they cut me from it!” he states with a laugh, speaking from an upmarket gym in central London with a street entrance so discreet it’s impossible to find without assistance. “I’d done the whole voice and everything — and they had me in the freezing sea getting baptized in a massive white gown. And they cut me!”.

Sources indicate that boyle even went to cinema to see the film, just to double-check. “I thought, maybe they put it in a flashback, or perhaps an end credit scene like Marvel movies.” They had not.

More than a decade on from this cinematic slight and his well-rehearsed rendition of Paisley’s booming baritone is yet to be utilized on screen. But audiences are now able to hear another accent Boyle’s been carefully crafting, and one that couldn’t be more different: the high-pitched, slightly nasal and mumbly voice of convicted crypto king Sam Bankman-Fried for “The Altruists,” out now on Netflix.

As it happens, since his Paisley faced the cutting room floor, Boyle — now 32 — has become TV’s go-to guy to play a wide assortment of other real-life people, both at home and abroad. At the same time as he’s swiftly risen up call sheets, over the last two years alone he’s stepped into the shoes of U.S. WWII navigator Harry Herbert Crosby in “Masters of the Air” and Abraham Lincoln’s assassin John Wilkes Booth in “Manhunt,” both for Apple TV, IRA commander Brendan Hughes in Hulu’s “Say Nothing” and brewery heir Arthur Guinness in Netflix’s “House of Guinness.”.

“I think I’ve played more real people than not,” he notes. “I’ve just got a very white, generic face — if you squint, you go ‘well, he sort of looks like him.’ It’s how I’ve stayed employed.”.

It has been revealed that there’s much more to it than that, though. Most of Boyle’s roles have been compromised and troubled individuals, sometimes cast via history as the villain. And yet he’s offered them nuance and a sense of vulnerability — serving up delicious shades of grey between the black and white.

Playing Sam Bankman-Fried — the mop-topped and scruffy former crypto poster boy now serving a 25-year sentence for stealing billions of dollars of customer funds — only cements Boyle’s status as one of the most exciting latest character actors around.

For all the headlines and eye-watering amounts of money, there was much grey area to explore.

As the show charts across its eight episodes, Bankman-Fried — alongside business partner, on-again off-again again love interest and fellow socially-awkward nerd Caroline Ellison (played to perfection by Julia Garner) — were followers of the “effective altruism” movement, and set out to use their tech wizardry to make a fortune and give most of it away. That’s not what happened, of course.

It has been revealed that “A crime was committed. People lost their jobs, families broke apart,” indicates Boyle. “But I do feel he was motivated by good. You know, the path to hell is paved with good intentions, and all the rest of it.”.

Boyle was prepping for what he describes as “that fucking accent that makes me sound like I’m on helium” months before he knew anything about “The Altruists.”.

In a bizarre coincidence, he’d been cast as Bankman-Fried in a different project, a film he says was “more of an Aaron Sorkin, ‘The Social Network’ thing.” Excited by the opportunity, he had dived into the research, soaking up the “hours of footage” of him online. “That guy loved an interview — so there was so much for me to pull from.” The accent he created was a cocktail of a “sort of lisp that kids have when they spend too much time on the PlayStation” and “Californian vowel sounds,” mixed in with some stuttering.

Boyle had even taken it out to test-drive on the streets, the streets in Bankman-Fried’s case being “World of Warcraft” and Magic: The Gathering conventions. He’d done similar things previously. Before playing Wilkes Booth in “Manhunt,” he had hung out with cowboys. “I love getting into who they are. That’s the most exciting part of the job,” he says.

But then, as movies so often do, it fell apart. He was distraught.

It has been revealed that months later, while shooting another film, he got a call — there was a different Sam Bankman-Fried project in the works, this time a series and at Netflix. Garner was already attached. “I was like, no, I can’t — my heart’s already been broken by this before. I’d spent months researching this guy.” But he read the script and found it “so funny and curious, it’s like a love story — and so different than the movie.”.

For an initial Zoom with creator Graham Moore and director James Ponsoldt, Boyle put his studies to good use, buying a jumper from budget retailer Primark and covering it in “Pot Noodle stains” and back-combing his hair to make it look as bushy as possible. He also introduced into character from the off. “I was like, ‘Hi guys, I’m just off the phone with Mark Zuckerberg, God that guy was keeping me forever,’” he notes in full Bankman-Fried tones.

Recent findings suggest that weeks later at the first screen test with Garner — “the best actor I’ve ever worked with… she’s so good,” claims Boyle — he was delighted to discover that she had the same approach. “I’d only ever seen her with a short pixie cut looking very beautiful, but she comes in with her wig on and the nose and teeth and her body language is so different — she’s awkward, bumping into people.” Realising what he was up against, he introduced himself as Sam, with the helium voice, and they immediately started talking in character.

As part of his deep dive into Bankman-Fried, Boyle was even able to speak to the man himself in prison (apparently in the “same cell block as P Diddy”). There had been plans to visit, but the convict had breached prison rules by giving Tucker Carlson an unauthorized interview and was moved from Brooklyn to LA. With the first week of filming already underway in Toronto in early 2025, there wasn’t time, so instead, via a temporary email address he was given, Boyle sent “well over 100 questions.” While he promised he wouldn’t reveal the contents of the exchange, he claims Bankman-Fried “answered most of them” and was “very forthcoming.”.

“You’re also just sort of bowled over immediately by his intelligence,” he says. “This is a guy who walks into rooms in dirty shorts and t-shirts and gets VCs to give him billions and billions of dollars.”.

But the billions of dollars weren’t what Boyle — who admits he’s never had any interest in crypto or wealth accumulation — wanted to ask about. “Knowing about financial crime doesn’t help me when I’m playing the role,” he indicates. “When I’m creating a character, what I’m interested in is like someone’s childhood and inner thoughts, feelings, hopes, dreams, nightmares, that kind of thing.”.

Earlier this year, Boyle was in Cannes with Clio Barnard’s “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning,” the film that he actually went off to make after the first Bankman-Fried project fell through.

A moving slice of Gen Z social-realism set and shot in the British city of Birmingham, the drama follows five close friends from the same council estate. Now reaching their 30s, they’re realizing that economic reality has largely thwarted whatever ambitions they once had. Boyle, who stars alongside fellow fast-risers Lola Petticrew, Joe Cole, Jay Lycurgo and Daryl McCormack, plays a frustrated and depressed father-of-two who, despite his university degree, finds himself forced to deliver takeaway food. It’s gritty and bleak at times, but filled with warmth, empathy and camaraderie (accompanied by comedy dancing when they start hitting the drinks).

For Boyle, it was “the kind of film that made me want to be an actor — when I watched films like ‘This Is England’ and ‘Quadrophenia’ and Ken Loach, films that have that political motivation.” As a kid from a working-class neighborhood himself, it was also a world and community he recognized, with the film reflecting the “love and light and people helping each other” that he remembers. Crucially, it wasn’t all grey skies and “people crying into cups of tea.”.

Industry observers note that barnard, he claims, was his first time being directed by a “real auteur.” She’s completely changed his outlook on acting. Whereas projects were previously selected based on his character, Boyle now says he “wants to work with people like her who have that vision and can create that kind of cinema.”.

“I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning” was also another chance to act alongside Petticrew, arguably the Emerald Isle’s other brightest latest talent and recently hailed for her chilling performance as a vengeance-seeking serial killer being chased by Emmy Rossum in Hulu’s “Furious.”.

It has been revealed that as it happens, Boyle and Petticrew grew up in the same part of Belfast and have been “besties” since they first met aged around 11 or 12. “We were just hanging out with each other on the streets, and then wanting to be actors and doing am-dram together,” he says. “We were the two little weirdos, because nobody else wanted to act.”.

Sources indicate that around the age of 15, they appeared together in a short film from director Mike Lennox called “Rough Deal” (Boyle played a drug dealer, Petticrew his little sister who then took the drugs and overdosed). “It was for schools or something,” claims Boyle. A little over 10 years later and Lennox, now an Oscar nominee and BAFTA winner, was one of the directors and exec producers on “Say Nothing,” FX’s drama about the Troubles. “And in his pitch deck, he had put forward Lola and I.”.

Boyle was asked to play the younger Brendan Hughes, one of leaders of the 1980 hunger strikes whose mural he walked past on his way to school, while Lola was up as the key role of IRA volunteer Dolours Price. They did the audition tape in Boyle’s mum’s living room.

It has been revealed that “We put her ironing board out and a few books of fucking Narnia and a John Grisham that my dad was reading and duct-taped my iPhone to a World’s Best Mum mug, and did it,” he says. “And that’s how we booked most of the jobs we’ve got. Lola always comes and helps me for a substantial job.”.

According to recent reports, “The Altruists” and “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning” (which recently won Boyle the joint best actor award at the Rome Film Festival) are the latest highlights in a career still very much in its ascendancy. But casting directors excited by what they see may have to form an orderly queue — his upcoming schedule is already stacked.

Sources indicate that the reason we’re talking from a swanky celeb-friendly gym in London isn’t because Boyle enjoys working out, but because he’s in the middle of shooting Sky series “Charmer,” playing a seducer-for-hire who tests the fidelity of his wealthy clients’ partners. There’s full-frontal scene, so he figured he should get in shape. “My character’s self-obsessed and goes to the gym every day, so it wouldn’t make sense if I was built like a cigarette,” he claims. Sky, thankfully, paid for extortionate gym fees.

Recent findings suggest that once “Charmer” wraps in January, Boyle’s back into bowler hat, booze and brawling territory for the second season of “House of Guinness.” He indicates there are two projects incoming afterwards, including a “tennis movie,” although he won’t offer any further details. Another feature, “The Worst” shot in France this past summer during the World Cup, is now in post. Boyle actually replaced fellow Belfast native Jamie Dornan (“Ireland’s best looking man”) in the dark comedy, in which he plays a name-dropping talent agent alongside Keira Knightley and Alicia Vikander.

And then there’s “Close to Home,” the aptly titled series that finally takes Boyle back to his roots. It’s his most personal project to date, about a graduate returning to post-Troubles Belfast and based on the novel by Michael Magee, which happens to be his favorite book. “There’s so many similarities to his life and mine, and it’s the first time I’d read something that felt like, Jesus Christ, these are thoughts only I thought I’ve had,” he notes, adding that Magee “sat next to my brother in school.”.

Sources indicate that but for “Close to Home” he’s not just the lead (and co-starring with another fast-rising local, “Kneecap” breakout Jessica Reynolds), but getting behind the camera too as his first executive producer credit. “It was great to be involved in the casting and location meetings and just every little thing you can think of — I just loved it,” he notes.

Shooting “Close to Home” in Belfast earlier this year coincided with Boyle actually moving back to his home town after a decade flitting between London and Latest York.

He’s triumphantly returned, 10 years after his Ian Paisley was deleted, now as a leading man, a celebrated chameleon who can seemingly take on any historical figure thrown at him — and their voice, no matter how high-pitched or nasal — and even a filmmaker in his own right.

Not that the old friends he’s getting to hang out with again seem to care.

“My best mate — my best mate in the world — hasn’t seen anything I’ve been in,” notes Boyle. “He says to me, I’ll watch you when you’re in a film with The Rock. That’s all he watches. He once tried to watch a period drama I was in and got about 10 minutes into it and was just like ‘This is so boring. There were no fights, no car chases.’ So we don’t speak about work.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.

The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.

The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.

It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.

The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.

As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.

He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup.".

Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.

In a recent development, his parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.

Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.

After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

#35905. Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1130 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary.
  • Now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds.
  • The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary. Unlike Earth, which has a relatively orderly magnetic field with clearly defined north and south poles, both distant planets possess strangely distorted and dramatically tilted magnetic fields. For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds. A new study suggests that changes in how well materials conduct electricity under extreme conditions could explain the planets' unusual magnetism. The findings also raise an intriguing possibility: the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change dramatically over just a few decades.

The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.

Why Uranus and Neptune Have Such Strange Magnetic Fields.

Sources indicate that planetary magnetic fields originate deep beneath the surface, where moving fluids capable of conducting electricity generate magnetic forces. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

On Earth, the dynamo operates within the outer core, a layer of molten metal surrounded by mostly solid rock. As liquid iron circulates and the planet rotates, it generates a magnetic field resembling that of a giant bar magnet. This produces the familiar north and south magnetic poles that allow compasses to point in a consistent direction.

In a recent development, earth's magnetic field is also closely aligned with its rotation axis. Its main magnetic axis, known as a dipole, is tilted by only 11 degrees. Uranus and Neptune are strikingly different. Uranus has a magnetic dipole tilted by 59 degrees, while Neptune's is tilted by 47 degrees.

Explaining these extreme tilts requires a better understanding of what lies inside the two planets.

According to recent reports, uranus and Neptune are classified as ice giants, a name that reflects their presumed composition rather than suggesting they are simply frozen worlds. Each is approximately four times wider than Earth, and scientists believe their interiors contain substantial amounts of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rocky material. However, their precise internal compositions remain uncertain.

Extreme Conditions Deep Inside the Ice Giants.

Chi Yan, the study's lead author and a research associate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences, believes the combination of the planets' enormous size and unusual chemical makeup may help explain their distorted magnetic fields.

Recent findings suggest that "Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," stated Yan. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.".

Recent findings suggest that ions are electrically charged particles that can carry electric current. If the materials inside Uranus and Neptune become more conductive at greater depths, that could significantly influence how their magnetic fields are generated.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed computer simulations designed to reproduce the strange magnetic fields recorded by Voyager 2.

Their models assumed that electrical conductivity increases deeper inside the planets. The researchers also tested a variety of possible internal structures, examining how circulating fluids, temperature changes, and magnetic forces interact over time.

The results suggest that these changing electrical properties could play a crucial role in producing the unusual magnetic fields observed around both ice giants.

Magnetic Poles Could Shift Dramatically Within Decades.

Perhaps the most surprising finding is that the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may be far less stable than Earth's.

In a recent development, according to the simulations, their magnetic axes could undergo substantial changes in relatively short periods. In some scenarios, the magnetic tilt shifted by tens of degrees within only a few decades.

That raises the possibility that the magnetic fields surrounding Uranus and Neptune today are significantly different from those measured when Voyager 2 flew past them in the 1980s.

In a recent development, "Earth's magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," remarked Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.".

Sources indicate that these dramatic changes remain predictions from computer models rather than confirmed observations. However, scientists may already have a way to look for evidence of them.

James Webb Telescope Could Reveal Magnetic Changes.

In a recent development, researchers are now examining detailed infrared images of Uranus and Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They are particularly interested in the planets' auroras, which form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in their atmospheres.

Recent findings suggest that auroras are closely connected to planetary magnetic fields, making them valuable clues to what is happening far above the planets' hidden interiors. Changes in the appearance and arrangement of these glowing atmospheric features could help researchers determine whether the magnetic poles have shifted since Voyager 2's encounters.

"We are busy working on what's contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere, promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone," said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign and reviewed the paper for the journal.

The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles. Its behavior is influenced by magnetic activity, offering another potential source of information about the planets' changing magnetic environments.

The research team hopes to combine Webb's auroral observations with Voyager 2's original magnetic field measurements and the fresh dynamo simulations. Together, these sources of evidence could provide the clearest picture yet of how the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are arranged today.

Sources indicate that even so, scientists emphasize that fully understanding the planets' deep interiors will require new spacecraft missions to these distant worlds. Until then, improved simulations and powerful telescopes may help unravel one of the solar system's most unusual magnetic mysteries.

The research was funded by The University of Texas Institute for Geophysics (UTIG) in the Jackson School of Geosciences, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and the Science and Technology Facilities Council.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buzz buzz, Yellowjackets hive! Season 4 is upon us, and we're ready to be dragged back into the creepy woods of teen chaos and middle-aged mayhem. The Season 3 finale offered some major moments, including the revelation of the Pit Girl's identity and Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) sending out a distress call to the civilized world.

Trailers for Season 4 have teased the titular soccer team's return home. However, if the first three seasons have taught us anything, it's that you can take the girl out of the wilderness, but you can't take the wilderness out of the girl. In both the past and present timelines, Shauna (Sophie Nélisse/Melanie Lynskey), Misty (Samantha Hanratty/Christina Ricci), and Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown/Tawny Cypress) are grappling for survival and control, so buckle up for a wild ride.

But hey, if the off-season has you feeling foggy on which teammates (and rivals) have bit the dust (or been bit up), we've got you covered with a recap of all the deaths in Seasons 1, 2, and 3.

And keep an eye on this space — the final season of Yellowjackets is sure to see more folks fall, and we'll be updating this list accordingly.

It has been revealed that also, wherever possible, we have images with sliders of before and after. Slide 'em if you can stomach it.

Having just moved up from the junior varsity team, Rachel has the grim distinction of being the first Yellowjacket to die. Like the plane's pilots, she died in the crash, from a laceration to her throat.

In a recent development, father of Travis and Javi, Coach Bill (Carlos Sanz) died as a result of the plane crash that dropped the team in the Canadian wilderness. He'd fallen out of the plane into a tree. In an added bit of brutality, he died in front of Travis, as the teen boy tried to save him from his painful perch in a tree.

It has been revealed that good Christian girl Laura Lee (Jane Widdop) died a hero. After the team found an intact plane in the wilderness, Laura Lee began reading the manual to figure out how to fly it. She eventually took off with her teddy bear Leonard — and her personal lord and savior Jesus — as her co-pilots. But the plane exploded in the air, killing Laura and the Yellowjackets' chance of sending out a member for help.

Industry observers note that the queen bee who couldn't hack it in the cabin, Jackie (Ella Purnell) froze to death while sleeping outside. And then she had the bizarre honor of becoming the first to be eaten by the team.

Travis's younger brother Javi (Luciano Leroux) would also be eaten, though the Yellowjackets weren't directly to blame for his death. While the team was hunting Natalie, Javi offered her a hiding place. But before they could get to safety, he fell through the ice of a frozen lake and died. From there, he was eaten.

Industry observers note that despite the best efforts of the team, Shauna's baby was stillborn. This was a sad one.

Sources indicate that remember when Misty made a friend? She and Kristen (who was dubbed Crystal the Pistol by the team) bonded in the wilderness over their shared love of music and Steel Magnolias. They grew close enough that Misty shared her secret about destroying the plane's emergency transmitter, which Kristen — understandably — judged. From there, Misty pushed her off a cliff, and proclaimed the girl "missing.".

Real talk: Ben (Steven Krueger) lived way longer than we expected. The plane crash severely damaged his leg, which Misty then amputated on the spot. And incredibly, he survived possible infection, likely starvation, and the burning down of the cabin. But he couldn't escape the Yellowjackets. In a kangaroo court, they convicted him for the cabin's fiery annihilation (despite Misty's best efforts of a defense), and Taissa was chosen to carry out the execution. However, this was not how Ben died. Instead, he was tortured with crippling violence and deplorable conditions — that is, until Natalie took mercy on him and stabbed him fatally in the heart.

Poor Edwin (Nelson Franklin) just wanted to study frogs with his colleague Hannah (Ashley Sutton) and their guide Kodiak (Joel McHale). But then he stumbled in the Yellowjackets camp as they were feasting on Ben's remains. And, well, Lottie welcomed him with an axe to the head. RIP Edwin.

After Edwin was killed, the Yellowjackets imprisoned his surviving friends like they did Ben. When Kodiak tried to escape, he wasn't ended by the girls but by Hannah, who stabbed him in the eye. This was Hannah's bid to show the girls she could be trusted to keep their secret. And it got her through the rest of Season 3 at least.

Yellowjackets began — to quote Sarah McLachlan — building a mystery by introducing the show with the death of the Pit Girl. Underdressed for the snowy weather, she raced through the woods, pursued by masked figures, and ultimately fell into a pit of spikes, which killed her. Season 3 revealed her identity: Mari Ibarra (Alexa Barajas), a persistent rival of Shauna's. Mari too was eaten.

How Travis (Andres Soto) died was a big mystery in Season 1, with a real bummer of a reveal. In the present, accidentally hanged himself while attempting to talk to the darkness. Lottie was supposed to save him but had a technical malfunction.

Sources indicate that in Season 1, Adam Martin (Peter Gadiot) was a mechanic who was having an affair with Shauna. But when Shauna began to suspect he had betrayed her, she stabbed him to death. His murder was covered up with the help of Misty, Nat, Taissa, and Jeff, because Yellowjackets are ride or die. (Sometimes both!).

Masquerading as a journalist, Jessica Roberts (Rekha Sharma) got on the wrong side of Misty Quigley, who fatally poisoned her with fentanyl-laced cigarettes.

Taisaa's family pet was murdered by Night Taissa. Then, his head was placed on creepy basement altar, which would prove a foreshadowing for Ben's fate.

In Season 2, Detective Kevyn Tan (Alex Wyndham) was put in the awkward position of investigating his former high school classmates as he looked into the disappearance of Adam Martin. When his search led him to Lottie's cult's headquarters, he was felled — not by a Yellowjacket! — but by one of their fans. Specifically, Walter Tattersall (Elijah Wood), a citizen detective who fell for Misty. As the two were talking, Walter subtly poisoned Kevyn with a laced hot cocoa.

Nat (Juliette Lewis) died in the Season 2 finale, and we're still not over it. Of all the survivors, she seemed the one who likely to succeed in escaping their past. Worse yet, she was killed by her friend, Misty.

According to recent reports, it was an accident. Misty was trying to kill one of Lottie's cult members, Lisa (Nicole Maines), but Nat intervened by throwing her own body in front of the syringe, which was filled with poison. However, Natalie's story continued in the flashbacks. And yet, that only promised to make her ending sadder.

Who killed Lottie Matthews (Simone Kessell)? Well, to the surprise of many, it wasn't Shauna. It was her daughter, Callie Sadecki (Sarah Desjardins). Sure, Callie and Lottie had bonded, no matter how much that enraged Shauna. But when Callie confronted Lottie about stealing the incriminating DAT tape from the Sadecki home, Lottie began saying cryptic things about how Callie was a child of the Wilderness' darkness. In a rage, Callie reacted by shoving Lottie down the stairs.

Industry observers note that taissa's high school paramour (Liv Hewson) rejoined to the fold to reignite their romance and proved a solid teammate (Lauren Ambrose) in the present timeline. But their bliss was punctured by Van's cancer diagnosis, and yet that was not how she died! Hopeful the whatever of the wilderness would save her if she sacrificed someone else, Van tried to kill Melissa (Hilary Swank), a ball-capped Yellowjacket who was long thought dead, but had resurfaced under weird circumstances.

It has been revealed that ultimately, however, Van decided not kill Melissa. And in response, Melissa fatally stabbed her and fled, leaving Taissa to bury Van in an unmarked grave. Naturally, she took the opportunity to cut her lover open and eat her heart.

Industry News: The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • In a recent development, 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report indicates.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

In a recent development, 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report indicates. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

In a recent development, however, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

Sources indicate that “The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

It has been revealed that jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, noted she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the firm rolled out and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

In a recent development, mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

In a recent development, “We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

Most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic noted. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

Recent findings suggest that the cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

It has been revealed that single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

According to recent reports, “Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

It has been revealed that however, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply challenges posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

According to recent reports, “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

Recent findings suggest that beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

According to recent reports, “Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” mentioned Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

Sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is currently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a organization on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is presently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high shows the scale of India's climate challenge.

Sources indicate that “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann remarked. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

In a recent development, and when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, indicates the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability problems) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she noted. “Market leadership is key.”.

In a recent development, in the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

Tech Report: My Assistant Scammed Me. Then Did Far Worse to Demi Moore.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hollywoodreporter

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In March of 2018, someone walked into a FedEx office in Beverly Hills to pick up a package addressed to Demi Moore.
  • This person wasn’t Moore’s assistant, though the badge mentioned otherwise.
  • Sources indicate that over the next three weeks, he’d charge nearly $170,000 to the card while Moore was in Idaho, unaware of what was happening back in Los Angeles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In March of 2018, someone walked into a FedEx office in Beverly Hills to pick up a package addressed to Demi Moore.

This person wasn’t Moore’s assistant, though the badge mentioned otherwise. He had never met the actress and had no legitimate reason to be collecting her mail. But he knew the tracking number, the original shipping address and exactly what was inside the package: Moore’s American Express Black Card.

Sources indicate that over the next three weeks, he’d charge nearly $170,000 to the card while Moore was in Idaho, unaware of what was happening back in Los Angeles. Related Stories Lifestyle Baby2Baby Gala Fetes Demi Moore and Raises Over $20M for the Cause TV 'Landman' Ups 4 Actors to Series Regulars as Season 3 Begins Filming.

And the person who walked out of that FedEx office with her card was someone I knew.

Sources indicate that david Matthew Read wasn’t what you would picture when you hear “mastermind criminal.” Blond-haired and blue-eyed with a dimple poking out of one cheek, he was disarmingly forthcoming, sweet and funny. We first met in 2011, when he was in his late 20s and I was in my early 40s. I needed help hanging curtains, and a friend introduced me to him as a friend from church. Soon, David was somewhere between my part-time assistant and bestie, helping me with everything from errands to booking travel to prepping for parties.

It was only once I’d given him access to everything — including my P.O. Box, where he picked up my mail for me — that the friend who’d introduced us told me that David had actually been in prison a few years earlier for committing bank fraud.

But, the friend assured me, David was so trustworthy now that the church let him use their credit card to buy décor for their office. And when I asked David about the fraud and prison sentence, he was so forthcoming, so lacking in excuses and so willing to admit he’d done something wrong that I immediately pushed his crime out of my head.

Sources indicate that still, a few months into our arrangement, I realized that as an underemployed freelance writer, I didn’t actually need an assistant. Also, something about David had begun to seem off; he’d claim to be able to do things he couldn’t, and I’d only realize this when he’d present the “finished” result — a website, an Ikea bookshelf, research — and it was so unfinished that I wouldn’t know what to even say.

When I let him know that I no longer had work for him, he was sweet and understanding; he drove off in his orange convertible Mitsubishi Eclipse, and I figured that was the end of that.

And it was — until a few months later, when I got a call from Citibank that I owed nearly $7,000 on a credit card bill. Positive that it was a mistake, I had the representative read off the card number.

“It’s not mine,” I responded, relieved.

Oh, but it was, she explained. It was an additional card on my account, issued in the name of David Read.

Industry observers note that as she read off the list of charges, I fell into a shame spiral. How could I have been stupid enough to give a convicted criminal so much access to my life?

I don‘t remember exactly what David said when I first confronted him, just that he initially denied everything and then rather promptly confessed. He told me he’d only done it because the church needed him to buy certain things and, as a convicted felon, he couldn’t get a credit card, and so he’d intercepted my credit card bill one day when picking up my mail and ordered a card in his name under my account.

Recent findings suggest that when I read out charges we both knew couldn’t have been made for even the loosest of churches — to, among other places, Good Microbrew, The Abbey, Mickey’s, Hooters, Malibu Family Wines, DMH Aesthetics and a dating website called Successful Match — he admitted that his motivation had nothing to do with the church. He’d just wanted a credit card and didn’t have another way to get one.

David didn’t cry or plead for forgiveness. He calmly explained that he’d never wanted me to be financially responsible, which is why he’d been paying the charges for months; he just needed some time to get some money together. In the end, the friend who’d introduced us paid off the credit card and told David to pay him back by making regular donations to their church. (David ended up leaving the church shortly after.).

And so David became a part of my past, the I-got-scammed-by-an-assistant story I eventually forgot about.

Sources indicate that until July of 2018, when the friend who’d introduced us sent me a link to an OK! magazine story that David had done something similar to Demi Moore.

Industry observers note that A few months ago, mainly out of curiosity, I decided to see if I could find David. It took roughly four minutes: I logged onto a public records website, plopped in his name and emailed the four potential email addresses it provided: Are you the David Read that once worked for me?

A few minutes later, “Hi Anna please give me a call,” with a phone number appeared in my inbox.

A few minutes after that, my cell buzzed with a text: “Is this Anna you just emailed me.”.

Recent findings suggest that I was surprised by how easy it had been to track down a guy who’d spent 55 months in prison. But I was even more surprised by the name and photo that popped up on my iPhone alongside the text.

David Read was now Taylor Read Madison. The person I’d known as a man was now living as a woman.

Three days later, I sat across from Taylor at Liberation Café in Hollywood, splitting a breakfast burrito, Alanis Morissette playing in the background. The blond hair, blue eyes and dimple remained, but the hair was now long and tucked into a ponytail, the nails were painted, the dimple was decorated with a dash of blush and she was wearing a smattering of jewelry — including a diamond wedding ring.

Recent findings suggest that taylor felt both familiar and unfamiliar. As I watched her whip a hook out of her white purse and latch it onto the table before daintily placing the purse on it to keep it from sitting on the ground, I couldn’t help but notice that she seemed nervous.

And, of course, she had every reason to be. She also had every reason to not want to make her story public. So why was she here?

To tell this story, it helps to go back to the beginning.

Pennington Gap, Virginia, is the kind of place where you might expect a woman to receive a hefty settlement when her husband died of black lung.

And that was indeed what happened to Caroline Rhea, Taylor’s maternal grandmother. Because of the settlement and the fact that she was “good with credit cards” (a fact Taylor tells me without a hint of irony), Caroline could shower the grandchild she raised with clothing that she might not have otherwise been able to afford.

Sources indicate that “My grandmother was a little bit over-caring,” Taylor states now. “I think she felt guilty that my mother wasn’t able to raise me, and so she overcompensated.” (Taylor Read Madison has given me permission to use her former name and pronouns when describing events that occurred before her transition.).

Recent findings suggest that from an early age, David learned that “stuff” could make up for things like having a mother who couldn’t take care of you and a father who wasn’t around. Even though David and his grandmother lived in a single-wide trailer, “people thought I lived a completely different life,” Taylor explains. He helped perpetuate the delusion by getting off the bus early so the other kids didn’t see where he lived.

Industry observers note that the fraud started innocently enough. When David was 19 and attending Mountain Empire Community College in Big Stone Gap, Virginia, he began dating a 50-something attorney named Sam (not his real name) and quickly moved into Sam’s three-story, six-bedroom house. After about a year, their relationship had cooled, and Sam actually moved a new boyfriend in. But the house was so chaotic and unstructured that instead of moving out, David just relocated to a different bedroom.

In a recent development, the chaos extended to Sam’s financial life. “Sam was terrible with money,” Taylor states. “He was paying off his credit cards with credit cards, just living well beyond his means. And he had me on all his cards.”.

Sources indicate that one day, it occurred to David that Sam probably wouldn’t even notice if David bought himself a car. And that’s how he ended up driving a 1995 Oldsmobile Aurora out to L.A., his pockets filled with roughly $6,000 that he’d accumulated slowly by making periodic ATM withdrawals from Sam’s account.

Sources indicate that david came to L.A. ostensibly to meet a guy he’d been talking to online, but when he arrived and learned that the guy still lived with his ex-boyfriend, he didn’t care. He’d made it to L.A., the shiny place he’d always wanted to come to — a place where you could entirely reinvent yourself so long as you dressed the part.

Sources indicate that “Why do you think God invented credit? For fabulous people like me.” Demi Moore (Jules) in St. Elmo’s Fire.

Industry observers note that scamming Demi Moore was never part of the strategy. It probably wouldn’t have ever happened if David hadn’t been doing a lot of meth and hanging out with a druggy crowd.

In a recent development, david had inadvertently stumbled upon the ideal project for a meth-using, tech-savvy guy with a history of credit card fraud: He got access to the account from Ray, downloaded what he found in the FedEx system and started cross-referencing names and addresses of cardholders using Google’s My Maps feature. Eventually, he was able to connect tracking numbers to people’s names, phone numbers, business names and addresses. (FedEx did not respond to repeated requests for comment.).

At first, he didn’t know why some names were marked “titanium.” Then he realized it was code for the coveted Black Card — also known as the Centurion card — an invitation-only program that allegedly requires a minimum annual spend of $500,000 and is noted to include everything from private jet arrangements and exclusive restaurant reservations to VIP treatment at luxury hotels. “I freaked out a little,” Taylor recalls. “I remember thinking, ‘What can I get with this? Everything.’ ”.

When David saw Demi Moore’s name on the spreadsheet with the word titanium next to it, he didn’t care about who it was. He just had an idea of how he could get his hands on her card. “Demi Moore wasn’t a target,” Taylor indicates. “She was a convenience.”.

In the back end of the FedEx database, David redirected her card from her business manager at Nigro Karlin Segal Feldstein & Bolno in Century City to a FedEx store in Beverly Hills.

“At the time, all you needed to pick up a card was the tracking number, the name it was going to and the original shipping address,” Taylor claims. For added insurance, David made himself a badge that noted he was an assistant at Moore’s holding firm, Pajama Party Productions. Once he knew the card had been sent, he parked his (fraudulently purchased) Mercedes E-Class in front of the FedEx store, walked in with his badge and announced he was there to pick up a package for Moore. The clerk handed it over.

Industry observers note that then David drove to a Century City parking lot and called a friend who had access to a black-market website. Within a few minutes (after sending the friend $8 through his Cash App), David had Moore’s Social Security number. He then called AmEx, claiming to be Moore, and provided the representative with the Social Security number to activate it.

Moore wasn‘t David‘s only victim. Taylor estimates that she stole between 25 and 30 other cards through the scheme and used them over a period of roughly 18 months to do everything from renting a Porsche 911 in Florida to eating caviar for the first time at Barton G. in West Hollywood to buying a Rolex.

(Taylor gave me a download of the names she found in the FedEx back end that were being sent Black Cards at that time, and while some of the names are recognizable — for example, the late billionaire owner of the Indianapolis Colts, Jim Irsay, and literary agent Esther Newberg — most are not.).

Out of all of David’s shopping sprees, the one he did on Moore’s card was definitely the most extensive. From March 8 through March 27 of 2018, he bought so many things that he can’t begin to remember them all, though he does recall that most of his shopping was done at Nordstrom, Saks Off 5th and Bloomingdale’s and that he bought Gucci shoes and Roberto Cavalli clothing. He also recalls making more quotidian purchases with Moore’s card at Rite Aid and Bed Bath & Beyond.

It has been revealed that this wasn’t, Taylor notes, a joyride meant to give a taste of the high life. Or at least it wasn’t only that. After acquiring a Birkin bag — which the Off 5th on La Cienega used to sell — “I’d carry it around for like three days just to feel bougie because I was like, ‘Oh my God, this is the life I want,’ ” she says. “Then I’d list it on Fashionphile because I needed to sell this stuff to have a place to stay and food and the basic necessities you need to survive.” She says she could expect to make $10,000 to $15,000 in cash for such an item.

David knew the scheme would eventually unravel. On April 5, 2018, he was stopping by the Extra Space Storage facility on Vine near the 101 — where he kept everything he bought before selling it — when two Secret Service agents followed him out and arrested him.

They’d gotten wind of his scheme because David had used his own Chase debit card to cover a balance on a Nordstrom purchase he’d made with Moore’s card. “I think I was trying to get caught,” Taylor says now. It was the Chase debit card, combined with the number of times David had called AmEx when the card would get turned down, that made AmEx catch on to what he’d been doing. (Moore, through her representative, declined to comment for this story.).

Recent findings suggest that within a few minutes of being arrested, David had told the agents everything. “I figured if I was just straight up about things, it would be a little less painful,” she says, adding, “One thing I can say about me is that if I’ve done something, I will cop to it.”.

In a recent development, david had only been in L.A. County jail for a few days when he met someone who mentioned he had a contact at OK! magazine. David called the contact — not, he indicates, because he wanted his name in the press but because “I was really over it all and felt bad. I also just wanted the money and wasn’t really thinking clearly.” (Taylor says the magazine paid her $500 for an interview.).

He spent nearly a year in pretrial detention — with a break where he was released and then arrested again — and ended up serving his sentence in FCI Phoenix from April 2019 through December 2022. He appealed for an early release — claiming that because he was HIV-positive, COVID exposure was dangerous — but was denied. David also claimed in his appeal that prison life was dangerous for someone who was nonbinary.

Gender identity wasn’t a upcoming struggle; David had grown his hair long, done laser hair removal and started wearing women’s clothes in early adulthood but stopped after moving to L.A. In mid-2017, David began taking testosterone blockers and estradiol after learning they could be simply procured from a doctor. Even while occasionally wearing women’s clothes, David states he still “passed” as a man. “The hormones hadn’t really kicked in,” Taylor says now.

Recent findings suggest that despite what Taylor claimed in her appeal, no one in jail gave her a hard time for her gender identity. She says that the hormones had started working and her features had softened, but “I think mostly I was confusing people. They were just like, ‘I think they dropped you off at the wrong location.’ ” Does that mean, I asked, that her appeal wasn’t honest?

In a recent development, “There were real concerns [about COVID],” she says. “We were literally having outbreaks left and right, and they didn’t know what the fuck was going on.”.

As for the abuse she supposedly feared she’d be subjected to, “my attorney wrote all that,” she says.

Once out and back in L.A., he got a list of resources from the Hollywood LGBT Center, which led her to an organization called the Trans Latina Coalition that was connected to a place called the Trans Wellness Center. It was after joining their reentry program that she began going by Taylor.

She also found a upcoming career, working as a case manager at Trans Wellness for eight months before jumping to Access to Prevention, Advocacy, Intervention & Treatment [APAIT], another nonprofit that provides homeless services, where she works as an employment specialist.

It has been revealed that but Taylor has bigger aspirations: She’s in the process of getting her bachelor’s degree in information technology and cybersecurity, with aims to pursue her master’s afterward. The reason for the degrees, she claims, is that American Express wants to hire her, but they told her they need to see that she’s “serious.” She indicates that AmEx would pay her “a substantial amount of money” to work in their fraud prevention department. American Express declined comment on this assertion.

Recent findings suggest that taylor also seems to be thriving in her personal life. In January 2024, she met an Ecuadorian man on Grindr, and they married in June of that year. Taylor, who quit meth in jail, quickly realized that her new husband was doing a lot of meth and told him she was serious about him but couldn’t be with him if he kept using after what she’d been through. According to Taylor, he quit cold turkey. (Taylor still drinks; during one of our Saturday afternoon Zoom interviews, she sipped whiskey with cherries.).

It has been revealed that still, to hear Taylor tell it, her life today is as innocent and pure as a brand-fresh Birkin. Whenever I question her about why I should believe anything she claims when she has lied to me and so many other people so successfully so many times, she doesn’t do a hard sell.

“I don’t deserve it [for people to believe me],” she tells me at one point. “I mean, I can only show people, right?”.

Perhaps the most surprising part of all is that after everything that happened between us, I would have thought I’d have a hard time sitting across from Taylor or having a series of Zooms with her. I’d imagined I’d be hiding my purse, blurring my background or worried for my safety. Instead, I felt the way I had the first time we met. I liked her.

When I tell her it doesn’t make sense to me that someone could spend more than 15 years committing fraud and then, without a spiritual epiphany, a 12-step program or some life-altering experience, become someone who works with the homeless and wants to end the kind of fraud she once perpetrated, she isn’t defensive. She just calmly attributes her change to therapy, transitioning and finally feeling comfortable with herself. “I think now I’m living authentically,” she says.

When I saw her photo in OK!, I thought I knew exactly where I fit in the story. I was one of the people Taylor had fooled before she got to Demi Moore. It hadn’t occurred to me that one day I’d want something from her again, or that what I’d want was her version of a story I’d spent years telling as mine.

I have no idea whether she’s reformed or not. Since watching You Can See Everything, I’ve been thinking a lot about how much likability plays into believing someone who has a history of dishonesty. The truth, so to speak, in this situation is that the same personality and candor that wooed me before seems to have worked all over again.

Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why

💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.
  • Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.
  • Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.

Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.

Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.

In a recent development, one of the most striking examples is found in the Grand Canyon, where rocks separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, as if some force or phenomenon removed the layers that geologists would expect to see in between. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity.

It's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana noted in a statement.

It has been revealed that "The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance.".

In a new study published in the journal Nature, Dhungana and study co-author Nicolas Flament investigated whether activity far below Earth's surface was to blame.

Using computer models, they explored how the slow circulation of hot rock within Earth's mantle may have affected the continents over hundreds of millions of years.

The results suggest that three major ancient continental regions (Laurentia (modern North America), Baltica (northern Europe) and North China were gradually pushed up during the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately one billion to 540 million years ago. This would have left vast areas of land exposed to weathering and erosion for long periods, allowing water, wind and other processes to wear away rock that had formed much earlier.

But removing the rock is only part of the puzzle. They also needed to explain why the gaps are still visible today.

Industry observers note that their models suggest that the same regions subsequently began to sink. As sea levels rose relative to the land, sediment accumulated over the older, eroded surfaces, creating the sharp divide between ancient and younger rocks that we can still see today.

Crucially, the researchers found that the timing of the simulated continental uplift and sinking was consistent with geological evidence from North America, northern Europe and North China. This suggests that movements deep within Earth's mantle may have played a major role in shaping the geological record we see today.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

In a recent development, daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.
