Breaking: Lack of early border controls made UK ‘extremely vulnerable’ to Covid, inquiry finds

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest report also states test-and-trace failures allowed virus to spread quickly and unchecked.
  • The lack of international border controls at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic left the UK in an “extremely vulnerable position”, an inquiry has concluded.
  • In the latest report from the Covid-19 inquiry, the chair, Heather Hallett, also mentioned failures to quickly introduce a test-and-trace system allowed the virus to spread “with deadly speed across the country, virtually unchecked”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest report also states test-and-trace failures allowed virus to spread quickly and unchecked.

UK politics live – latest updates.

The lack of international border controls at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic left the UK in an “extremely vulnerable position”, an inquiry has concluded.

In the latest report from the Covid-19 inquiry, the chair, Heather Hallett, also mentioned failures to quickly introduce a test-and-trace system allowed the virus to spread “with deadly speed across the country, virtually unchecked”.

Sources indicate that she said: “The UK entered the Covid-19 pandemic woefully ill-prepared to implement effective, nationwide test, trace and isolate systems. This left decision-makers effectively blind to the scale of the highly contagious virus.”.

The report said years of public health emergencies and pandemic preparedness exercises should have meant the country was fully prepared to deploy test and trace; instead, a system had to be created “virtually from scratch” during a fast-moving emergency.

More than £25bn was spent on the NHS test-and-trace system in England but Lady Hallett said it had come too late and at a huge cost.

The Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice group mentioned the report had “once again exposed lies and incompetence”.

Industry observers note that “On 3 March 2020, Boris Johnson told us Britain had ‘fantastic testing systems’ and was ‘extremely well prepared’. That was a lie. Nine days later, his government stopped community testing as the virus spread,” it stated. “Those responsible for failures that cost lives should be stripped of any honours they hold. They have no place in public life.”.

Hallett also criticised the lax international border controls at the start of the pandemic, saying they had left the nation vulnerable for months.

The report said that by April 2020, 93% of countries had put in measures such as flight suspensions, border controls and travel restrictions, but the UK government was only asking travellers from high-risk areas, including Wuhan in China, where the virus originated, to self-isolate.

This policy did not prevent a coach of tourists from Wuhan entering England and travelling to Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland in February 2020, it mentioned, and there were no further restrictions until June.

Hallett said: “The decision to allow virtually unrestricted international travel in the first six months of 2020 came at a time when the UK had no mass testing or widespread contact tracing, and its healthcare resources were stretched thin.

“Overall, the UK was left in an extremely weak position from which to face the rapidly rising rates of infection.”.

The report said 18 February 2020, when there were only nine confirmed cases of Covid-19 in the UK, would have been the ideal time to bring in travel restrictions – when there were low levels of domestic infection, but higher rates elsewhere.

The 240-page report on test, trace and isolate is the seventh of 10 to be published by the Covid-19 inquiry, now the most expensive public inquiry in history with costs rising to more than £200m.

It is based on oral evidence from 41 witnesses in public hearings in May, as well as 200 written statements and more than 23,000 documents.

In previous reports, Hallett concluded that government failures caused Covid to spread “like wildfire” among vulnerable and elderly people in care homes, and that bringing in a lockdown a week earlier than happened could have saved more than 20,000 lives.

Hallett’s recommendations in this report included the creation of a UK-wide digital contact-tracing tool, better plans on how to deliver manual contact tracing at scale, and financial support for people to self-isolate.

Alan McNally, a professor of microbial genomics at the University of Birmingham, told the inquiry that if there was another pandemic in the near future, “in terms of delivering tests, we’ll be exactly where we were at the start of 2020”.

Covid-19 Families for Justice mentioned the country was “still dangerously unprepared”.

In a recent development, “Laboratories built during Covid have closed and equipment has been sold off. Ministers must fund a permanent testing network, give local teams the staff to trace outbreaks and make sure anyone asked to isolate can afford to stay home,” they said. “We cannot wait for another pandemic to rebuild the systems needed to protect us.”.

Hallett remarked a better test, trace and isolate system would be “fundamental to saving lives and reducing suffering” with the next deadly virus.

Tech Report: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.
  • The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence.
  • In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.

Recent findings suggest that "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that it's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

Sources indicate that more than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in Upcoming York and two in Wisconsin.

Recent findings suggest that the commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, remarked Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action proposal in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz stated in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

Sources indicate that the decision also poses a newly introduced test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles.".

Industry observers note that "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.".

Sources indicate that CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

According to recent reports, "We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood mentioned in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.".

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

Sources indicate that the U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

#35794. Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1147 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance.
  • In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.
  • The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. Latest research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.

The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an notable role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," noted Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

How Scientists Simulated Overtraining.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

Sources indicate that for the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

Recent findings suggest that after the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours.

In mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This showed that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

The more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

This prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than swiftly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

However, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

Dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

It has been revealed that according to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

In a recent development, another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

According to recent reports, this result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body.

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

Industry observers note that excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The newly introduced results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another important part of this process.

According to recent reports, for recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

Recent findings suggest that rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he currently works as a researcher.

Recent findings suggest that additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

Sources indicate that the team is now participating in a newly introduced international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

#35792. Tech Report: Would Ukraine trade land for NATO membership or protection?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (893 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Would Ukraine trade land for NATO membership or protection?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US has asked Ukraine whether it would be willing to cede Donetsk province to Russia in return for NATO membership.
  • So far, no concrete proposal had been put forward, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
  • Industry observers note that the Ukrainian leader stated the US was talking about guarantees similar to those enshrined in Articles 4 and 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, though did not envision US troops on Ukrainian soil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has asked Ukraine whether it would be willing to cede Donetsk province to Russia in return for NATO membership. Together, Donetsk and Luhansk constitute the so-called Donbas region. Russia right now controls most of Luhansk province, and large swathes of Donetsk, though Ukraine continues holding a number of major cities there, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.

So far, no concrete proposal had been put forward, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said he would publicly discuss the matter once the US and NATO member states had agreed on the strategy, stressing that he could not make any such decision "on his own." Zelenskyy also said any potential agreement would go ahead "without recognizing Russia's occupation of these territories.".

Industry observers note that the Ukrainian leader stated the US was talking about guarantees similar to those enshrined in Articles 4 and 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, though did not envision US troops on Ukrainian soil. Article 4 provides for consultations among member states in the event of imminent threats, while Article 5 stipulates that an attack on one state is considered an attack on all. The US, however, has said it pictures bilateral guarantees for Ukraine similar to those established with Israel and certain Middle Eastern countries.

Russia has yet to comment on these proposals, with President Putin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stating that "we maintain our position that, in the interest of the peace process, it is not appropriate to disclose details of the talks between us and the Americans.".

Experts interviewed by DW are skeptical of the land-for-security-guarantees idea, objecting that the US cannot uphold such an arrangement on its own.

Industry observers note that "It seems to me that this is what happens to normal diplomacy when it's been run by real estate agents who are used to selling people something that doesn't really exist," Oleksandr Kraiev of the North America-Israel Research Program at Ukraine's Ukrainian Prism think tank tells DW. He states that at least half of NATO's member states have reservations about Ukraine's accession.

"We'll just end up with a second Budapest Memorandum, it'll just carry a different name," Kraiev told DW. The original 1994 Budapest Memorandum stipulated that Russia, the US and UK respect Ukraine's independence and sovereignty in its existing borders and refrain from the threat or use of force to change its territorial integrity. Ukraine in return committed to giving up all nuclear weapons.

The Budapest Memorandum, however, did not contain any commitment by the UK or US to defend Ukraine in the event of an attack.

Most experts interviewed by DW are critical of the idea of holding a referendum to let ordinary Ukrainians decide whether their country should hand over full control of Donetsk province in exchange for NATO membership.

Industry observers note that this is because ceding territory would not only violate Ukraine's constitution and harm its national interests, but would also undermine a world order "in which borders cannot be redrawn by force," Oleksandr Khara of Ukraine's Centre for Defence Strategies told DW. "It doesn't matter whether the citizens of Ukraine vote for or against such a proposal," Khara stated, adding that any such referendum would set "a very dangerous precedent.".

A survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KISS) conducted between October 8 and 16 found that 61% of respondents categorically reject withdrawing troops from Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donbas, such as cities like Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, even in exchange for US and European security guarantees. 35% of respondents mentioned they would begrudgingly accept a land-for-security deal.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Defense analyst Khara doubts a bilateral agreement between Ukraine and the US, akin to those established between the US and Israel, would guarantee Kyiv any more support than it presently receives.

"This concerns financial support, joint weapons production and development, and the training of Ukrainian troops — everything that falls below the threshold of collective security," Khara told DW. "It is good that these commitments — security agreements, political declarations, and the allocation of funds in the budgets of the countries supporting us — are set out in writing, at least for the next five years." Yet to prevent another war, Khara believes that ideally, Ukraine needs "a nuclear shield," specifically, a "strategic one from the US" and a "tactical one from Europe.".

It has been revealed that ukrainian experts already floated to the idea of an alternative security arrangement to NATO members in December 2023, says Sergiy Solodkyy of Ukraine's New Europe research center. The arrangement would see Ukraine join the alliance within its internationally recognized borders, though specific protocols would stipulate that only territories under Kyiv's control would be defended.

This arrangement could be modeled on the German case, where West Germany became a member of NATO first, while East Germany joined the alliance only after German reunification.

In a recent development, west Germany never gave up on reunification, Solodkyy told DW. "That means we, too, should not give up on our territory or recognize the border." That is why he notes the land-for-security deal proposed to Ukraine is unacceptable.

"This is a trap that Russia and the US negotiators are trying to lure the Ukrainian side into," Solodkyy told DW.

Lawyer calls for urgent review of Letby convictions after expert witness revelations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Failure to disclose Peter Hindmarsh’s exclusion from practice raises ‘fundamental questions’ over nurse’s case.
  • Lucy Letby’s lawyer has remarked the court of appeal must urgently review her convictions, after it was revealed that a key medical witness in the prosecution’s case was barred from treating patients because of safety concerns.
  • The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh – a crucial expert witness who provided an opinion at Letby’s trial that two babies had been poisoned with insulin – was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023 because his hospital considered him unsafe to treat children in relation to insulin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Failure to disclose Peter Hindmarsh’s exclusion from practice raises ‘fundamental questions’ over nurse’s case.

Lucy Letby’s lawyer has remarked the court of appeal must urgently review her convictions, after it was revealed that a key medical witness in the prosecution’s case was barred from treating patients because of safety concerns.

The Guardian revealed this week that Prof Peter Hindmarsh – a crucial expert witness who provided an opinion at Letby’s trial that two babies had been poisoned with insulin – was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023 because his hospital considered him unsafe to treat children in relation to insulin.

The jury in the case were never told of the restriction placed on Hindmarsh, who was described by the prosecution in court as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.

Letby’s lawyer Mark McDonald, who has applied to the miscarriages of justice watchdog, the Criminal Cases Review Commission, for Letby’s convictions to be referred back to the court of appeal, said: “These revelations about Prof Hindmarsh, and the failure to disclose material information about him to the defence at trial, raise fundamental questions, and it is more urgent than ever that the court of appeal re-examines the safety of all Lucy Letby’s convictions.

“She is an innocent woman in prison, serving whole-life sentences, yet material information that could have been of critical importance to her defence was not disclosed. Did the police know? How did this information remain undisclosed?

Industry observers note that “We need answers. Lucy deserves answers. She should not have to spend another day behind bars while these fundamental questions remain unanswered.”.

Two senior lawyers noted serious concerns about an expert’s professional abilities, and non-disclosure to the defence, could be grounds for an appeal against convictions.

Letby’s defence lawyers were never told that Hindmarsh had been excluded from clinical practice, nor of an April 2023 tribunal ruling imposing a restriction. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has also said it was not informed.

It has been revealed that letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, and sentenced to 15 whole-life terms in prison. Hindmarsh’s opinion that two babies were poisoned with insulin, for which Letby was found guilty of attempted murder, was considered crucial to Letby being convicted. Court of appeal judges turned down her applications to appeal.

Since the convictions, dozens of leading UK and international medical and scientific experts have contributed to reports submitted with her CCRC application, arguing that the prosecution’s medical case, including Hindmarsh’s evidence, was wrong.

This week a Guardian investigation revealed that while the trial was going on, Hindmarsh’s employer barred him from clinical practice, and reported to the General Medical Council (GMC), which was already investigating him, that it believed he posed a risk to the safety of child patients.

According to recent reports, hindmarsh was a consultant paediatric endocrinologist – a specialist in hormones, including insulin – at University College London hospitals trust (UCLH) when the trial began. He had also been an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital.

In March 2023, while the trial was continuing at Manchester crown court, Dr Tim Hodgson, a medical director at UCLH, wrote to the GMC: “On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Prof [Hindmarsh] to practise clinically even under supervision … I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Prof Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people even with close clinical supervision.”.

Recent findings suggest that hodgson set out safety concerns, including two cases in which he remarked Hindmarsh had advised child patients to stop taking insulin. The GMC then applied for Hindmarsh’s registration as a doctor to be suspended, which Hindmarsh opposed. His barrister argued it would be disproportionate, and would impede his ability to work as an expert witness in legal cases.

Industry observers note that on 21 April 2023, a medical practitioners tribunal declined to suspend Hindmarsh but ordered that he must be directly supervised in his clinical work. That appears to have had no practical effect because UCLH had barred him from treating patients at all.

According to recent reports, hindmarsh did tell Cheshire constabulary, which instructed him in the case, about the GMC investigation in December 2022, and the CPS informed Letby’s defence team, but stated it would oppose the jury being told. The jury was never informed that the GMC had launched an investigation into concerns about Hindmarsh, referred by UCLH and Great Ormond Street. His contract at Great Ormond Street had been terminated in July 2022, and the jury was not told about that either.

Nick Johnson KC, the lead prosecution barrister, described Hindmarsh to the jury on 23 February 2023 as “the pre-eminent expert in that narrow field” of insulin.

Letby’s defence team was not informed about the further developments of March and April 2023, including that Hindmarsh had been excluded from clinical practice; and the jury was never told.

McDonald said: “It is staggering that Hindmarsh was presented as the pre-eminent expert on insulin at the trial, gave crucial evidence alleging babies were poisoned with insulin – which many eminent experts say was wrong – and it was never disclosed that he was considered by his own hospital [to be] unsafe to treat children with insulin, and barred from clinical practice.”.

A representative of Hindmarsh declined to answer questions from the Guardian, including whether he had failed to disclose the March and April developments to Cheshire constabulary. The police force declined to comment. The CPS confirmed it was never given the information.

According to recent reports, the criminal procedure rules require expert witnesses to disclose to the party instructing them anything, including disciplinary proceedings, “that might reasonably be thought capable of undermining the expert’s opinion or detract from the credibility or impartiality of the expert”. The rules were introduced in 2014 after recommendations by the Law Commission to improve expert evidence and guard against miscarriages of justice.

In a recent development, the commission was set up after a series of notorious miscarriages of justice based partly on flawed evidence from medical expert witnesses. The cases included Sally Clark, a solicitor who was wrongly convicted in 1999 of killing her two infant sons.

Recent findings suggest that clark’s convictions were overturned in 2003 after a CCRC referral to the court of appeal, principally because key medical evidence had not been disclosed to the defence. A striking statistical opinion presented by an expert witness for the prosecution, about the likelihood of both sons dying, was also shown to be catastrophically wrong. Clark had spent more than three years in prison condemned as a child killer and never recovered from her ordeal; she died in 2007 of acute alcohol poisoning.

Tim Green KC, a specialist in disclosure, said of the rules: “If there was a failure to make relevant disclosure of material undermining an expert’s opinion evidence, and where that opinion evidence was relevant to the central challenges before the jury, then that failure could form part of the grounds of appeal. It all depends upon the facts of a particular case and potential weight of the non-disclosure upon the jury’s verdict.”.

Industry observers note that pete Weatherby KC, a barrister with extensive experience of criminal trials, said: “The expert witness disclosure rules are there to protect the integrity of the trial process and avoid miscarriages of justice. Expert evidence was pivotal in the Lucy Letby prosecution because there was no direct or forensic evidence that she committed any of the criminal acts of which she was accused.

“Serious concerns about an expert’s conduct or judgment may be highly relevant to assessing their expertise, credibility, and the reliability of their evidence. If those concerns were not before the jury, that could be very significant for an appeal. If the full details were not obtained by the prosecution, and disclosed to the defence at the time, that would be even more significant.”.

#35787. This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (927 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared.
  • In a recent development, during the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different.
  • Industry observers note that the newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. The strange animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has also received a name with a personal connection to the two student scientists who helped identify it.

In a recent development, during the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different. Instead of a modern city, the landscape was a warm, swampy river delta populated by giant insects, early animals adapted to life on land, and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways. This environment supported an extraordinary variety of life, leaving behind fossils that now provide a remarkable glimpse into Earth's prehistoric past.

Industry observers note that the newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. Its name means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek," honoring the mothers of the two student researchers, both of whom are named Jean. The discovery is described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

A 309-Million-Year-Old Fossil With Extraordinary Detail.

The Mazon Creek fossil deposits are among the world's most important sources of Carboniferous fossils, in large part because of the conditions that existed when the animals were alive.

Sources indicate that as plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment swiftly covered their remains. This rapid burial created ideal conditions for fossilization, sometimes preserving delicate structures that would ordinarily disappear long before they could become fossils.

"What's really cool about Mazon Creek is that it preserves all of these unusual details -- things like toe pads and body outlines," states Allison Sefcovic, co-lead author of the paper and 2025 Women in Science intern at the Field.

"In the fossil of Jeanerpeton, we can see some of the scales on its back and tiny 'belly ribs' called gastralia. You can even see the eye impressions! It's so cool to see.".

Industry observers note that these exceptionally preserved features offer valuable evidence of what early amphibian relatives looked like. They also indicate that several anatomical characteristics associated with modern frogs and salamanders were already present approximately 309 million years ago.

A Prehistoric Species Hidden in Plain Sight.

Although Jeanerpeton mazonensis has only recently been formally described, its fossil was discovered many years earlier. An amateur fossil collector originally found the specimen and later donated it to the Field Museum.

When researchers first examined it, they classified the animal as Amphibamus grandiceps, a previously established species known from the Mazon Creek area. However, closer examination eventually revealed that the fossil represented a distinct animal.

Misidentifications like this can occur when scientists have limited information about ancient species. Fossils that appear similar are sometimes assigned to an existing species even when notable differences have not yet been recognized.

Paleontologists refer to such broad classifications as a "waste bin taxon." The term describes a category in which multiple fossils are grouped together because they seem related, even though their true identities and evolutionary relationships remain poorly understood.

"What we're finding from the Field Museum's collection are a bunch of things that historically were grouped together into this waste bin taxon known as Amphibamus grandiceps," states Cam So, co-author on the study and postdoctoral researcher at the Field Museum.

Industry observers note that "Jeanerpeton is one of those species. And now, we've found enough evidence to support it being an anatomically distinct animal. With this publication, we officially pull Jeanerpeton out of this waste bin taxon.".

Recent findings suggest that the finding highlights how museum collections can continue to produce discoveries long after fossils are first collected. In this case, a specimen already held by the Field Museum provided enough anatomical evidence to establish a separate species.

Two Student Scientists Make a Remarkable Discovery.

The research was co-led by Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who participated in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. The initiative encourages young women to explore careers in scientific research and museums.

Both students worked alongside So as members of the research group led by Arjan Mann, the museum's assistant curator of fossil fishes and early tetrapods in the Negaunee Integrative Research Center.

For Kohlberg, the project offered an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar scientific field and gain confidence through hands-on research.

In a recent development, "Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," says Kohlberg. "My experience at the Field and in the Women in Science program has made me more confident in my abilities to try something fresh. It is scary to take on a project when you feel like you don't know as much as you should, but I learned with my practical experience that it is possible to overcome that fear with hard work.".

The identification of Jeanerpeton mazonensis adds another species to the growing record of ancient life preserved at Mazon Creek. As researchers continue examining fossils from the region, each discovery helps reveal more about the extraordinary diversity of animals and plants that inhabited Illinois more than 300 million years ago.

#35784. Breaking: Scientists found a star inside of another giant star

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (906 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Scientists found a star inside of another giant star

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have detected a star slightly less massive than the sun inside a giant star for the first time.
  • The two stars, in the nearby Andromeda Galaxy, had circled each other for thousands of years.
  • Scientists think the same kind of spiral explains how many star pairs end up circling each other very closely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have detected a star slightly less massive than the sun inside a giant star for the first time.

The two stars, in the nearby Andromeda Galaxy, had circled each other for thousands of years. Then the giant swallowed the smaller star. The trapped star took only about seven years to spiral to the center, where the two merged into a single star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope supplied the final evidence.

Scientists think the same kind of spiral explains how many star pairs end up circling each other very closely. In this case, the small star didn't survive. But in other pairs, the giant's gas gets blasted away first, leaving both stars in an orbit that takes just hours or days instead of years. Those tight pairs can later become black holes or super-dense dead star cores called neutron stars, or explode as supernovas. Some also send out gravitational waves, which are ripples in space and time.

Lead author Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University, and an international team reported the discovery Wednesday in the journal Nature.

The researchers nicknamed the larger star "Significant Bao," and it earned the name. It had about seven times the sun's mass and 350 times its width, shining 18,000 times brighter.

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," stated Karel Temmink, a doctoral student at Radboud University in the Netherlands, in a statement.

Its partner, "Little Bao," had about 70 percent of the sun's mass.

Stars like Substantial Bao swell up near the end of their lives. If our sun did the same, it could grow past Earth's orbit. As Big Bao swelled, Little Bao began skimming its outer layer and stripping away gas. Soon the small star was orbiting inside the giant. The gas there was spread so thin that Little Bao stayed intact for years, according to the paper. Still, the gas slowed it down, much like air slows a thrown ball, until it eventually sank toward the giant's core.

No telescope can literally see inside a star. But friction from the small star's plunge churned the giant's gas and carried that heat to the surface. There it highlighted up as seven years of steady brightening. When the team compared the starlight from before and after the eruption — and tested computer models against it — the best explanation was a small star spiraling inside the giant.

It has been revealed that when the smaller one finally reached the giant core, gravity likely ripped it apart. That triggered a blast that hurled about one-tenth of the giant's outer material into space.

Their encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," mentioned Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia.

The explosion itself came on surprisingly fast. The team thought an outburst would take years. Instead, it took just a week from when its brightness started rising to its peak, said Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain.

Scientists expect many star pairs to go through this phase, but catching one in the act has taken incredible luck.

"The timescales involved are short, months to years, and the rates at which they form are low," astrophysicist Jason Nordhaus wrote in a commentary published alongside the study. "Just a few stars exist in this phase at any given time in a galaxy such as the Milky Way.".

Astronomers usually piece together star mergers long after they happen. This time, a fleet of telescopes followed Bao as the events unfolded. The team first noticed the star acting strangely in Feb. 2023, in data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. In Sep. 2024, another telescope saw it brightening and puffing out dust. In July 2025, NASA's Spherex telescope happened to catch it fading in visible light while it brightened in infrared light. Then, on Oct. 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility, a sky-scanning telescope in California, spotted the eruption.

Sources indicate that webb took its look on Dec. 24, 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. No telescope had ever followed up on an event like this so quickly, Karambelkar mentioned.

Sources indicate that what the newly single star, now just called "Bao," will become remains an open question. Only future observations will show how it settles down.

According to recent reports, NASA's newly introduced Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile will scan huge areas of sky over and over. They should spot events like this in hundreds of nearby galaxies.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar noted.

Industry News: UN warns against misuse of security laws as UK weighs Palestine Action ban

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Human rights committee publishes guidance on freedom of association, which criticises vague laws targeting ‘extremism’.
  • The UN human rights committee has warned against the misuse of counter-terrorism and national security legislation as the UK’s highest court considers the lawfulness of the ban on Palestine Action.
  • In its first comprehensive guidance on freedom of association, the committee criticises vaguely worded laws targeting “extremism” or “undesirable” organisations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Human rights committee publishes guidance on freedom of association, which criticises vague laws targeting ‘extremism’.

The UN human rights committee has warned against the misuse of counter-terrorism and national security legislation as the UK’s highest court considers the lawfulness of the ban on Palestine Action.

In its first comprehensive guidance on freedom of association, the committee criticises vaguely worded laws targeting “extremism” or “undesirable” organisations.

While the document, published on Thursday, does not explicitly refer to Palestine Action, Hélène Tigroudja, the vice-chair of the committee, said the decision to glitch the guidance on freedom of association had been spurred by events in countries including the UK, North Korea, Russia, China and Israel.

She said there were accepted grounds for restricting the exercise of freedom of association, such as national security and the fight against terrorism, but added: “These legitimate purposes are too often so vaguely defined by domestic legislation, and more importantly, so extensively misused by authorities to silence by way of criminalising associations such as climate activists, children and young-led movements, human rights defenders, journalists, trade unionists, that these aims must be used with a heightened caution.

“In this regard, what is observable at a global level, is the abuse of the ‘terrorism’ rhetoric to target associations and/or their members and to expose them not only to public opinion’s criticism but also to sanctions, including criminal punishment such as heavy fines or arrest and detention for the individuals.”.

Last year’s decision to ban Palestine Action has been criticised by civil liberties groups, politicians of different stripes, a former director of public prosecutions and a former director of the security services.

Palestine Action was the first direct action group to be banned under the UK Terrorism Act, placing it alongside the likes of al-Qaida and Boko Haram. In the supreme court case, its aims was described by its lawyer as: “disruption of the supply of weapons from the United Kingdom to Israel at a time when the international court of justice (“ICJ”) had found ‘a real and imminent risk [of] irreparable prejudice’ to the rights of Palestinians in Gaza not to be subjected to acts of genocide”. Israel denies committing war crimes or genocide.

The UN human rights committee guidance states: “The right to defend human rights, the reporting of human rights violations, or the advocacy for accountability, for instance, cannot as such be labelled as a threat or breach of public order.”.

The decision of the supreme court as to whether the ban on Palestine Action was lawful is awaited after it heard a challenge to proscription earlier this month, on the basis that it disproportionately interfered with the rights to freedom of speech and protest.

Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action who brought the legal challenge, said of the committee’s report: “This goes to the heart of the Palestine Action case. The government cannot simply label a movement ‘terrorist’ and use that designation to suppress political dissent by extinguishing the fundamental rights of its members and supporters.

“I urge the supreme court to heed this clear warning and overturn this unjust, dangerous and disproportionate ban. If the courts fail to uphold these fundamental freedoms, we will take our case to the European court of human rights. The criminalisation of direct action protest has no place in a democracy, and we will not stop fighting until this Orwellian proscription is overturned.”.

The Home Office has been approached for comment.

#35779. Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same.
  • It has been revealed that the study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles.
  • Industry observers note that when sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same. Researchers at Adelaide University have now identified a surprising reason for this dramatic change, offering insights that could help make hydrogen-powered stoves, ovens, and other household appliances safer and more dependable.

It has been revealed that the study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles. Sea salt transported inland by the wind is one notable source.

Industry observers note that when sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow. But when sodium concentrations fall, the flames become much harder to see, even though the burner continues operating under the same conditions.

This discovery has crucial implications for the development of hydrogen appliances. Instead of depending on flame color to show whether a burner is running, engineers may need to incorporate other detection technologies. Improving these systems could help support the adoption of hydrogen as a lower-emissions alternative to natural gas.

Why Hydrogen Flames Change Color With the Weather.

Lead researcher Professor Paul Medwell, from the School of Electrical and Mechanical Engineering at Adelaide University, explained that studying hydrogen flames under ordinary environmental conditions is essential for developing appliances that people can safely and confidently use at home.*.

"Hydrogen has significant potential as part of a lower-emissions energy future, and we need to understand how it behaves in the real world if we want people to be confident using it.

"Our research helps explain why hydrogen flames can look different from one day to the next. That knowledge gives engineers valuable information to develop appliances and flame-detection systems that work reliably, regardless of changing environmental conditions.".

To investigate these changes, the researchers combined controlled laboratory experiments with outdoor testing around Adelaide. They examined how hydrogen flames responded to variations in atmospheric conditions, including shifting weather patterns and changes in the air reaching the burner.

It has been revealed that over two weeks, the team monitored light emissions from hydrogen flames while keeping the burner settings unchanged. Despite the consistent operating conditions, the sodium-related light signal varied by more than 28 times between its lowest and highest recorded values.

Weather played a major role in those differences. Air that had passed over the ocean generally contained more sodium, producing flames with a stronger orange glow. When the air carried less sodium, the flames appeared considerably fainter.

Hydrogen Flames Are Harder to See Than Natural Gas Flames.

The researchers also examined how hydrogen flames compared with those produced by a conventional natural gas cooktop.

They found that hydrogen flames emitted less visible light on average, even when atmospheric conditions favored a brighter flame. This difference presents an additional challenge for appliances that use visible flames to indicate whether a burner is operating.

Hydrogen combustion can also produce faint blue and red light. However, the researchers found that these colors were easiest to detect in darkened surroundings, making them less useful as reliable visual indicators under everyday lighting conditions.

Together, the findings show why judging whether a hydrogen burner is operating based on appearance alone may be unreliable. A flame that is clearly visible under one set of conditions could become extremely difficult to detect when the surrounding air changes.

Making Hydrogen-Powered Homes Safer.

Medwell emphasized that the results do not undermine hydrogen's potential as an energy source. Instead, they demonstrate why appliances must be engineered to accommodate the fuel's particular properties.

"Different energy sources have different properties, and good engineering is about understanding those differences and designing for them.

"Rather than relying on a flame looking a particular color, we can investigate other ways of confirming that a burner is operating. Options include specialized ultraviolet or infrared flame detectors and temperature sensors.

"By identifying the factors that influence flame visibility, we can help inform the development of hydrogen appliances that are fit for purpose in real homes and other everyday settings.".

Such detection systems could provide a more dependable way to confirm that hydrogen is burning, regardless of whether its flame appears orange, faint blue, or is barely visible.

It has been revealed that by identifying how environmental sodium affects flame visibility, the research provides information that engineers can use when designing hydrogen appliances for kitchens and other everyday environments. That knowledge could help make the technology safer and more practical as interest in lower-emissions energy alternatives grows.

The project brought together researchers from Adelaide University, the University of Newly introduced South Wales, and Gas Infrastructure Research Australia. Support came through the Future Fuels Cooperative Research Centre, with funding provided under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program.

The study, 'The role of sodium on hydrogen flame visibility in domestic settings,' was published in Next Energy.

Recent findings suggest that *In 2023, the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) introduced Australia's first 100% hydrogen-powered home in Victoria. The demonstration demonstrated that household gas appliances could operate entirely on hydrogen, a development described as a 'game changer'.

FAA pauses installation of fresh routers after ground stop

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Aviation Administration stated Tuesday it would pause the installation of latest routers after problems with the technology led the agency to matter a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration stated Tuesday it would pause the installation of latest routers after problems with the technology led the agency to matter a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have noted they are working to figure out the root cause of the glitch and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

Sources indicate that the senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the latest devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, noted Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

In a recent development, "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he noted. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

Recent findings suggest that duffy dismissed the idea that the router problem had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and stated it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best headphones shouldn't be the ones that bring on credit card debt.
  • These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.
  • Recent findings suggest that especially as we head into the holiday season and Black Friday deals heat up, it can be tempting to grab the $450 flagship headphones on sale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best headphones shouldn't be the ones that bring on credit card debt. As a professional headphone reviewer, I'm partial to a pair of well-executed flagship headphones, but I don't always find the $450 price point practical for most folks — especially when you can often find headphones for literally hundreds of dollars cheaper that perform 80 percent as well.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Recent findings suggest that especially as we head into the holiday season and Black Friday deals heat up, it can be tempting to grab the $450 flagship headphones on sale. And yes, I always recommend squeezing all the value you can, but great sales also mean mid-range headphones that are already under the $300 mark at full price are not only likely to drop to $200 or less — they already have. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

With that in mind, I rounded up my three favorite pairs of headphones under $300 that I tested in 2026. I also included one bonus option in honor of the holiday sale season.

Check out our full review of the Sony XM4C headphones.

Sources indicate that anyone looking for the best blend of sound, comfort, and price: Sony brought back its viral XM4 headphones with the second-generation XM4Cs. The design remains unchanged from the first generation, but sound gets a boost, making them the best-sounding headphones under $300 I've tried, and a no-brainer for students, office workers, or anyone looking to get as close as possible to the flagship headphone experience, minus the price.

It has been revealed that plenty of $450 headphones don't feature 10-band equalizers. Sony's WH-1000XM4C headphones do. That stated, even if you don't like to mess around with a companion app, these headphones sound balanced and rich out of the box, making everything from classical piano concertos to classic rock shine. While their sound quality is certainly a huge draw, it's far from the only standout feature of these headphones.

It has been revealed that sony struck simplistic gold with the design of the XM4 headphones in 2020 — which is why some fans were sad to see the iconic look go in the XM5 and XM6 headphones. Now, prospective buyers don't have to decide between the latest tech and the coveted XM4 design. While Sony didn't add any improvements to the ANC (it still features the same four mics and QN1 processor it did in 2020), the internals of the sound quality make these a much easier (and easier to get) recommendation in 2026. Like the OG XM4s, these headphones also are relatively low profile, with plenty of cushioning in the headband and ear cups, minus any overbearing squeeze. The result is solid passive noise cancellation, with comfort enough to get you through a work or school day's worth of wear.

The biggest cons of these headphones are that they lack spatial audio and the battery life got bumped down three hours from the first to the second gen — 30 to 27 hours. However, the 27-hour range still sits above other (more expensive) mid-range options, so it's not the most devastating loss. And at full price, they're still less than half the price of Sony's other 2026 release: the ultra-premium 1000X the Collexion headphones.

Check out our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

People who like their headphones to make a statement: The Nothing Headphone (a) are going to turn some heads. The rectangular ear cup and semi-transparent design meld together the past and the future in a way that is unmistakably Nothing. Don't get me wrong, though; they don't just look good. These headphones pack a relatively balanced soundscape and decent ANC.

They're also the perfect headphones for anyone who isn't too great about plugging their devices in regularly, as they pack a whopping 75 hours of listening time per charge, with the ANC on.

These are the best headphones Nothing makes, thanks to their combo of performance and value, and the value prop here is strong. When brainstorming the best headphones under $300, the Headphone (a) immediately came to mind because they offer something most budget-oriented headphones don't (or can't, due to budget constraints): an unmistakable style. These headphones aren't trying to dupe any other one on the market.

Instead, Nothing uses the more plastic-heavy design to its advantage, securing a cool retro look, all the while offering four colorways: White, black, pink, and yellow. The power of the design doesn't stop there. The on-ear controls of these headphones are so intuitive, both in their function and placement, that I rarely reached for my device when wearing them.

Sound-wise, these aren't going to blow you away — there are likely better options for sound quality and ANC around this price point. But they get the job done, and likely won't make you regret making a decision based on aesthetics. They're a little fussy to carry around, but with headphones that look this good, I'm betting most folks will want to wear them more often than not.

On sale, these headphones have dropped as low as $109, giving them a truly impressive value prop.

Check out our full review of the Soundcore Space 2.

It has been revealed that bargain hunters: If you're looking for the cheapest possible option that will still offer a mid-range experience, the Soundcore Space 2 headphones are the way to go. With sound, comfort, and an overall experience that punches above its price point, I recommend these headphones to anyone looking to spend less than $200.

According to recent reports, as nice as the XM4C headphones are, they're still an investment. These Soundcore headphones keep performance high on the core features of headphones, while showing their price point in places that don't detract too much from the overall user experience.

Let's start with how they wear. The memory foam cushions are plush, and the headphones themselves squeeze enough to offer some passive noise cancellation and stay secure, without skewing into headache-inducing territory. In other words, I could wear them for hours at a time without concern. The on-ear controls were great too, with buttons easy to find blindly and use for playback. The look isn't half bad either — at a glance, you could almost mistake them for a pair of Beats.

The sound and active noise cancellation did the job. On the former front, it came out balanced, if a bit unremarkable. Still, that's not a knock at this price point — they could sound a lot worse. ANC-wise, these feel like great daily drivers, but maybe not the satisfactory answer for anyone who has extra noisy neighbors, co-workers, or lives near a construction site. A plane ride, however? Yeah, these will do the job just fine.

My biggest warning on the sound front? Without audio playing, I could hear some minor squeaking while moving my head around, but not every single time. Not ideal, but certainly not a dealbreaker, either.

Check out our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd gen).

Frequent travelers, those who prioritize comfort, and anyone who happens to catch a sale: The thing about Bose is they're going to make an incredibly comfortable pair of headphones, and the second-generation QuietComforts are no exception. I wore these headphones through long work and travel days, and they felt comfortable the entire time I wore them — glasses, earrings, and all.

It has been revealed that the only major catch? At full price, they don't fall into the under-$300 criteria. That mentioned, I've seen them fall below that price point thanks to sales enough times that they at least deserve an honorable mention spot on this list.

Industry observers note that similar to the Sonys, these Bose headphones verge on the premium headphone experience. This is especially the case thanks to the balanced sound and presence of spatial audio, which narrows the gap between the $450 Bose QC Ultra headphones and these. The active noise cancellation is some of the best available, and while I dealt with some clipping on especially loud noises (think plane engines during takeoff or trains screeching up to the platform), for the most part these headphones give the cocoon of silence to expect from Bose.

Industry observers note that I used them while flying up the west coast, and found them to be the perfect travel headphones. Though they're on the shorter side of battery life, it was still plenty to last me through my trip, and that was with heavy wear during the travel days — these headphones are comfortable enough to simply keep on. While better equalizer options would truly take these headphones over the top to more premium territory, the Bose QCs make up for it in other areas. The replaceable ear cups, for instance, mean that you can extend the life of your headphones once they start to wear down. And while the price point is on the higher side, grabbing them on sale makes them one of the best value finds in the headphones market, especially if you prioritize comfort and noise cancellation above all else.

Industry observers note that bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for three years at Mashable.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Pentagon did not release any information on Hegseth's trip or confirm the visit, although it was broadcast on Venezuelan state media.
  • It has been revealed that the visit comes after US forces in January ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and took him along with his wife to New York to face drug trafficking charges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Venezuela on Wednesday, met with the country's interim authorities and also signed a military cooperation deal with the Latin American country.

The Pentagon did not release any information on Hegseth's trip or confirm the visit, although it was broadcast on Venezuelan state media.

It has been revealed that the visit comes after US forces in January ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and took him along with his wife to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Since then, US President Donald Trump has backed acting President Delcy Rodriguez to lead the country.

Both Rodriguez and Hegseth touted the fresh military agreement between the two countries at the presidential palace in Caracas.

Rodriguez said the deal would strengthen training for the Venezuelan military while facilitating access to new technologies. She said this would allow the two nations to "face common threats.".

Hegseth remarked the US sees the deal "as a reestablishment of our defense partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries.".

The agreement includes intelligence sharing between the two nations in addition to joint training.

The Pentagon chief stated the US seeks "to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders.".

Hegseth said Wednesday that since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.".

It has been revealed that US-Venezuela relations were strained under Maduro, who had taken office in 2013. In 2019, Maduro cut off Venezuela's formal diplomatic relations with the US after Trump's first administration recognized Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaido as the country's interim president.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that after the ouster of Maduro, the Trump administration urged Venezuela to comply with demands such as US access to the Venezuelan oil market. Trump had threatened Rodriguez, who was Venezuela's vice president, with a "fate worse than Maduro" if she didn't cooperate with Washington.

Trump has later praised Rodriguez as a "terrific person" who is doing a "great job.".

Recent findings suggest that under Rodriguez, Venezuela has released political prisoners and facilitated the shipments of oil to the US, with the US then controlling the proceeds and returning the money under an energy deal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been overseeing Venezuela's transition and is in close contact with Rodriguez.

Elections after Maduro's ouster are expected at some point in Venezuela, but with Rodriguez's government acting favorably towards the US, it's unclear whether they would happen anytime soon. Nobel Prize winner and opposition leader Maria Corina Machado recently urged elections after arriving in Venezuela.

#35773. Latest Update: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
